children.title: Eigenvalue Geometry of Positivity
children.top_down_role: Definite, semidefinite, singular, and indefinite spectral regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue Geometry of Positivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral classification of real symmetric matrices by the signs of their eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) have ordered eigenvalues \(\lambda_1(X)\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_n(X)\). Then \(X\succ0\) exactly when \(\lambda_n(X)>0\), and \(X\succeq0\) exactly when \(\lambda_n(X)\geq0\). A positive-semidefinite matrix is singular exactly when \(\lambda_n(X)=0\). The matrix \(X\) is indefinite exactly when \(\lambda_1(X)>0>\lambda_n(X)\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\) equals the number of nonzero eigenvalues counted with multiplicity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positivity, semidefiniteness, singularity, indefiniteness, and rank are determined completely by the signs and multiplicities of a symmetric matrix’s eigenvalues.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real symmetric \(n\times n\) matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\succ0\iff\lambda_n(X)>0\), \(X\succeq0\iff\lambda_n(X)\geq0\), and \(X\) is indefinite iff \(\lambda_1(X)>0>\lambda_n(X)\).

children.title: Matrix-Order Monotonicity Calculus

children.title: Löwner Order Comparisons
children.top_down_role: Comparability, strict ordering, and order intervals for symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Löwner Order Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-form and spectral characterizations of the Löwner partial order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A,B\in\mathbb S^n\), define \(A\preceq B\) when \(B-A\succeq0\). Equivalently, \(A\preceq B\) if and only if \(x^{\mathsf T}Ax\leq x^{\mathsf T}Bx\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), or if and only if \(\lambda_{\min}(B-A)\geq0\). Likewise, \(A\prec B\) means \(B-A\succ0\), equivalently the quadratic inequality is strict for every nonzero \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One symmetric matrix is below another in Löwner order exactly when their difference is positive semidefinite, equivalently when every quadratic form comparison holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\preceq B\iff B-A\succeq0\iff x^{\mathsf T}Ax\leq x^{\mathsf T}Bx\text{ for all }x\in\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: A is below B in Löwner order

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-semidefinite order and basic Löwner-order calculus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consolidates the extract's positive-(semi)definiteness foundations and its order, eigenvalue, congruence, and inverse-order properties while preserving the failed converse for eigenvalue comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For A\in\mathcal S^n, A\succ0 exactly when all eigenvalues of A are positive, equivalently x^TAx>0 for every x\ne0; and A\succeq0 exactly when all eigenvalues are nonnegative, equivalently x^TAx\ge0 for every x. The sets \mathcal S_{++}^n and \mathcal S_+^n are convex, with \mathcal S_+^n a convex cone. For A,B\in\mathcal S^n, define A\succeq B iff A-B\succeq0 and A\succ B iff A-B\succ0. The relation \succeq is the Löwner partial order. If A\succeq B, then \lambda_i(A)\ge\lambda_i(B) for 1\le i\le n, but these componentwise eigenvalue inequalities do not imply A\succeq B. For every S\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}, A\succeq B implies S^TAS\succeq S^TBS; if \operatorname{rank}S=m, then A\succ B implies S^TAS\succ S^TBS. The corresponding converses hold when S is square and nonsingular. If A\succ0 and B\succ0, then A\succeq B if and only if B^{-1}\succeq A^{-1}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive (semi)definiteness is characterized equivalently by eigenvalues or quadratic forms. The positive-semidefinite cone induces the Löwner partial order. This order implies ordered-eigenvalue inequalities, although the converse fails; it is preserved by congruence with the stated rank conditions, and matrix inversion reverses it on positive definite matrices.
assumptions_latex: S\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\ \text{nonsingular for the congruence converses}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A\succeq B\Rightarrow\lambda_i(A)\ge\lambda_i(B)\ (1\le i\le n)\ \text{with no converse in general};\quad A\succeq B\Rightarrow S^TAS\succeq S^TBS;\quad A\succ B\Rightarrow S^TAS\succ S^TBS\ \text{if }\operatorname{rank}S=m;\quad A\succeq B\Longleftrightarrow B^{-1}\succeq A^{-1}\ \text{when }A,B\succ0.

children.title: Operator-Monotone Matrix Maps
children.top_down_role: Matrix-function regimes that preserve Löwner ordering.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Monotone Matrix Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional operator monotonicity on a real interval, uniformly across matrix sizes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) be an interval and let \(f:I\to\mathbb R\). The function \(f\) is operator monotone on \(I\) if, for every \(n\geq1\) and all \(A,B\in\mathbb S^n\) whose spectra lie in \(I\), functional calculus satisfies \(A\preceq B\Rightarrow f(A)\preceq f(B)\). Requiring this implication only for one fixed size \(n\) defines matrix monotonicity of order \(n\), which is generally weaker.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar function is operator monotone when its spectral matrix functional calculus preserves Löwner order in every matrix dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(f:I\to\mathbb R\) is defined on every relevant eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\preceq B\Longrightarrow f(A)\preceq f(B)\) in every dimension.

notation.meaning: matrix obtained by applying f to the eigenvalues of A

children.title: Order-Preserving Congruences
children.top_down_role: Congruence-based transformations viewed through matrix-order preservation.

knowledge_statements.title: Order-Preserving Congruences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation and, for invertible maps, reflection of Löwner order under congruence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(A,B\in\mathbb S^n\), \(A\preceq B\), and \(C\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), then \(C^{\mathsf T}AC\preceq C^{\mathsf T}BC\). If \(m=n\) and \(C\) is invertible, congruence also reflects order: \(C^{\mathsf T}AC\preceq C^{\mathsf T}BC\) if and only if \(A\preceq B\). Positive definiteness is preserved when \(C\) is invertible but may be lost when \(C\) is rank deficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Congruence maps preserve Löwner order; invertible congruences preserve it in both directions and retain positive definiteness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\preceq B\Rightarrow C^{\mathsf T}AC\preceq C^{\mathsf T}BC\), with equivalence when \(C\) is square and invertible.

notation.meaning: congruence transformation of A by C

children.title: Courant-Fischer Variational Eigenvalue Principle
children.top_down_role: Minimax and extremal-eigenvalue viewpoints used in SDP geometry and modeling.

children.title: Courant–Fischer Minimax Characterization
children.top_down_role: Subspace-based minimax organization of ordered eigenvalues.

knowledge_statements.title: Courant–Fischer Minimax Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional minimax characterization for eigenvalues ordered from largest to smallest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb S^n\) have eigenvalues \(\lambda_1(A)\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_n(A)\). For every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\),
\[
\lambda_k(A)=\max_{\substack{S\leq\mathbb R^n\\ \dim S=k}}\ \min_{\substack{x\in S\\ \lVert x\rVert_2=1}}x^{\mathsf T}Ax
=\min_{\substack{T\leq\mathbb R^n\\ \dim T=n-k+1}}\ \max_{\substack{x\in T\\ \lVert x\rVert_2=1}}x^{\mathsf T}Ax.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each ordered eigenvalue equals both a maximum-over-subspaces of minimum Rayleigh quotients and a dual minimum-over-subspaces of maximum Rayleigh quotients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_k(A)\) equals the two stated subspace minimax values.

notation.meaning: S is a linear subspace of Euclidean space

children.title: Extremal Eigenvalue Variational Geometry
children.top_down_role: Optimization viewpoints for largest and smallest eigenvalues.

knowledge_statements.title: Extremal Eigenvalue Variational Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rayleigh-quotient representations of the largest and smallest eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(A\in\mathbb S^n\),
\[
\lambda_{\max}(A)=\max_{\lVert x\rVert_2=1}x^{\mathsf T}Ax,
\qquad
\lambda_{\min}(A)=\min_{\lVert x\rVert_2=1}x^{\mathsf T}Ax.
\]
A unit vector attains the maximum exactly when it belongs to the eigenspace of \(\lambda_{\max}(A)\), and it attains the minimum exactly when it belongs to the eigenspace of \(\lambda_{\min}(A)\). Consequently, \(A\preceq tI\) exactly when \(\lambda_{\max}(A)\leq t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extreme eigenvalues are the extreme Rayleigh quotients, and their optimizers are precisely unit vectors in the corresponding eigenspaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\max}(A)=\max_{\lVert x\rVert_2=1}x^{\mathsf T}Ax\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(A)=\min_{\lVert x\rVert_2=1}x^{\mathsf T}Ax\).

children.title: Invariant-Subspace Regimes
children.top_down_role: Subspace structure associated with extremal spectral values and multiplicities.

knowledge_statements.title: Invariant-Subspace Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical invariant subspaces in Courant–Fischer formulas and multiplicity-induced ambiguity at spectral cutoffs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb S^n\) have an orthonormal eigenbasis \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\) with \(\lambda_1(A)\geq\cdots\geq\lambda_n(A)\). In the max–min Courant–Fischer formula for \(\lambda_k(A)\), the invariant subspace \(S_k=\operatorname{span}\{u_1,\ldots,u_k\}\) is optimal. In the min–max formula, \(T_k=\operatorname{span}\{u_k,\ldots,u_n\}\) is optimal. The leading spectral subspace \(S_k\) is independent of the choice of ordered eigenbasis when \(k=n\) or \(\lambda_k(A)>\lambda_{k+1}(A)\), while the trailing spectral subspace \(T_k\) is independent of that choice when \(k=1\) or \(\lambda_{k-1}(A)>\lambda_k(A)\). When a cutoff passes through a repeated-eigenvalue eigenspace, rotations within that eigenspace yield different optimal invariant subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Leading and trailing spectral subspaces attain the Courant–Fischer extrema. A gap at the relevant cutoff makes the corresponding spectral subspace independent of the eigenbasis, while multiplicity at the cutoff permits different optimal invariant subspaces.
assumptions_latex: \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\) is an eigenbasis ordered by nonincreasing eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_k\) and \(T_k\) attain the respective Courant–Fischer extrema, with eigenbasis-independent spectral subspaces under the stated cutoff gaps.

children.title: Eigenvalue-Based Convex Functions
children.top_down_role: Convex scalar constructions built from ordered eigenvalue data.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue-Based Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity transfer from symmetric scalar functions to spectral functions on symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, and invariant under coordinate permutations. For \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), let \(\lambda(X)\) be the vector of eigenvalues in nonincreasing order and define \(F(X)=f(\lambda(X))\). Then \(F\) is a convex, lower-semicontinuous function on \(\mathbb S^n\) and is orthogonally invariant: \(F(Q^{\mathsf T}XQ)=F(X)\) for every orthogonal \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric convex scalar function of the eigenvalue vector induces a convex, lower-semicontinuous, orthogonally invariant matrix function.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, convex, lower semicontinuous, and permutation invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=f\circ\lambda\) is convex, lower semicontinuous, and orthogonally invariant on \(\mathbb S^n\).

children.title: Unitarily Invariant Matrix Functions
children.top_down_role: Matrix functions determined by spectral data and invariant under orthogonal changes of basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Unitarily Invariant Matrix Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral representation of orthogonally invariant functions on real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(F:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is orthogonally invariant, meaning \(F(Q^{\mathsf T}XQ)=F(X)\) for every orthogonal \(Q\), if and only if there exists a permutation-invariant function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) such that \(F(X)=f(\lambda(X))\). One may take \(f(a)=F(\operatorname{Diag}(a))\); permutation invariance makes the representation independent of eigenvalue ordering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on symmetric matrices is orthogonally invariant exactly when it is a symmetric function of the matrix’s eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(Q^{\mathsf T}XQ)=F(X)\) for all orthogonal \(Q\) iff \(F(X)=f(\lambda(X))\) for some permutation-invariant \(f\).

notation.meaning: diagonal matrix with diagonal vector a

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Davis convexity theorem for orthogonally invariant matrix functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes convexity of an orthogonally invariant real-valued function on symmetric matrices through its restriction to diagonal matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:\mathcal S^n\to\mathbb R satisfy F(U^TAU)=F(A) for every A\in\mathcal S^n and every orthogonal matrix U. Then F is convex if and only if its restriction to diagonal matrices is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonally invariant real-valued function on symmetric matrices is convex exactly when its restriction to diagonal matrices is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is convex}\iff F|_{\operatorname{Diag}(\mathbb R^n)}\text{ is convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Von Neumann representation of unitarily invariant norms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes real matrix norms invariant under orthogonal left and right transformations using symmetric gauge functions of singular values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A norm \|\cdot\| on \mathbb R^{n\times n} is unitarily invariant if and only if there exists a symmetric gauge function f on \mathbb R^n such that \|X\|=f(\sigma(X)) for every X\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}, where \sigma(X)=\lambda\!\left((X^TX)^{1/2}\right).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unitarily invariant norms on real square matrices are exactly those obtained by applying a symmetric gauge function to the singular-value vector.
assumptions_latex: \|\cdot\|\text{ is a norm on }\mathbb R^{n\times n}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\cdot\|\text{ is unitarily invariant}\iff \exists\text{ a symmetric gauge }f\text{ such that }\|X\|=f(\sigma(X))\ \forall X

children.title: Matrix Convexity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between scalar spectral convexity and matrix-order convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix Convexity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar convexity does not imply operator convexity across matrix dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Operator convexity on an interval \(I\) requires
\[
f(\theta A+(1-\theta)B)\preceq \theta f(A)+(1-\theta)f(B)
\]
for every matrix size, all symmetric \(A,B\) with spectra in \(I\), and \(0\leq\theta\leq1\). This is strictly stronger than scalar convexity. In particular, \(f(t)=t^4\) is scalar convex on \(\mathbb R\) but is not operator convex there. More sharply, any real polynomial that is operator convex on all of \(\mathbb R\) has degree at most two.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matrix convexity is stronger than scalar convexity: the convex scalar polynomial t-to-the-fourth is not operator convex, and globally operator-convex polynomials have degree at most two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scalar convexity alone does not imply the displayed Löwner-order inequality in every dimension.

notation.meaning: spectral functional calculus applied to A
interval on which operator convexity is tested

children.title: PSD Cone Self-Duality
children.top_down_role: Self-dual organization of the positive-semidefinite cone under trace pairing.

knowledge_statements.title: PSD Cone Self-Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Self-duality of the positive-semidefinite cone under the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Equip \(\mathbb S^n\) with the trace inner product \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(XY)\), and let \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\). Its dual cone is
\[
K^*=\{Y\in\mathbb S^n:\langle X,Y\rangle\geq0\text{ for every }X\in K\}.
\]
Then \(K^*=K\). Equivalently, a symmetric matrix \(Y\) is positive semidefinite exactly when \(x^{\mathsf T}Yx=\langle xx^{\mathsf T},Y\rangle\geq0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the trace inner product, the dual cone of positive-semidefinite matrices is the positive-semidefinite cone itself.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^n\) carries the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathbb S_+^n)^*=\mathbb S_+^n\).

notation.meaning: cone of real positive-semidefinite n-by-n matrices
dual cone defined by nonnegative inner products

children.title: Polar-Cone Pairing
children.top_down_role: Polar relationships surrounding semidefinite feasibility and separation.

knowledge_statements.title: Polar-Cone Pairing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual and polar conventions for the PSD cone under trace pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a cone \(K\) in an inner-product space, define its nonpositive polar by \(K^\circ=\{Y:\langle X,Y\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }X\in K\}\). Since \(K^\circ=-K^*\), self-duality of \(K=\mathbb S_+^n\) gives
\[
(\mathbb S_+^n)^\circ=-\mathbb S_+^n.
\]
Thus \(Y\) pairs nonpositively with every positive-semidefinite \(X\) exactly when \(Y\preceq0\). Under the alternative convention calling the nonnegative set the polar, that set equals \(\mathbb S_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the nonpositive polar convention, the PSD cone’s polar is the negative PSD cone; with the nonnegative dual convention, it is self-dual.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^n\) carries the trace inner product.
The polar uses the nonpositive-pairing convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathbb S_+^n)^\circ=-\mathbb S_+^n\).

children.title: Orthogonality Faces
children.top_down_role: Facial structures selected by orthogonality under semidefinite pairing.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonality Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real PSD cone with the trace pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(Y\in\mathbb S_+^n\), define \(F_Y=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\langle X,Y\rangle=0\}\). Then
\[F_Y=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:XY=0\}=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{range}(X)\subseteq\ker Y\}.\]
Moreover, \(F_Y\) is the face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) exposed by the supporting functional \(X\mapsto\langle X,Y\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PSD matrices orthogonal to a fixed PSD matrix form an exposed face, consisting exactly of matrices whose ranges lie in the fixed matrix's kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_Y=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{range}(X)\subseteq\ker Y\}\), and \(F_Y\) is an exposed face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\).

notation.meaning: Real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices of order n.
Face exposed by Y through orthogonality.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\succeq0\) if and only if \(X=V^{\mathsf T}V\) for some real matrix \(V\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A matrix \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) is positive semidefinite if and only if there exist an integer \(k\geq0\) and vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^k\) such that
\[X_{ij}=v_i^{\mathsf T}v_j\quad(1\leq i,j\leq n).\]
Equivalently, if \(V\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}\) has columns \(v_i\), then \(X=V^{\mathsf T}V\). The least possible \(k\) equals \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric matrix is PSD exactly when it is a Gram matrix of real vectors; the smallest vector dimension equals the matrix rank.

children.title: Low-Rank Factor Coordinates
children.top_down_role: Rectangular factor parameterizations exposing rank structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(X)\leq r\) if and only if \(X=UU^{\mathsf T}\) for some \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\).

notation.meaning: Real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices of order n.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rectangular factor coordinates for bounded-rank PSD matrices.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(0\leq r\leq n\),
\[\operatorname{rank}(X)\leq r\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X=UU^{\mathsf T}\text{ for some }U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}.\]
Moreover, \(\operatorname{rank}(X)=r\) exactly when such a factor \(U\) has full column rank. If \(U,V\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) both have full column rank and \(UU^{\mathsf T}=VV^{\mathsf T}\), then \(V=UQ\) for some \(Q\in O(r)\). Thus full-rank factors are coordinates modulo right orthogonal transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: PSD matrices of rank at most r are exactly products UU-transpose; at exact rank r, full-column-rank factors differ only by an orthogonal transformation.
knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Factor Coordinates

children.title: Principal Matrix Square Roots
children.top_down_role: Canonical square-root representations and their spectral organization.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There is a unique \(X^{1/2}\in\mathbb S_+^n\) satisfying \((X^{1/2})^2=X\).

notation.meaning: Principal positive-semidefinite square root of X.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Principal square root of a real PSD matrix.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.4 Positive definite matrices p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\) have a spectral decomposition \(X=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}\), where \(Q\) is orthogonal and \(\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\) with \(\lambda_i\geq0\). Then
\[X^{1/2}=Q\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_n})Q^{\mathsf T}\]
is independent of the chosen spectral basis, belongs to \(\mathbb S_+^n\), and satisfies \((X^{1/2})^2=X\). It is the unique positive-semidefinite matrix with this square, and \(\ker(X^{1/2})=\ker(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every PSD matrix has a unique PSD square root, obtained by taking nonnegative square roots of its eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.title: Principal Matrix Square Roots

children.title: PSD Congruence-Automorphism Geometry

children.title: Positivity-Preserving Congruences
children.top_down_role: Congruence actions preserving positive semidefiniteness.

knowledge_statements.title: Positivity-Preserving Congruences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Possibly rectangular real congruence maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\),
\[A^{\mathsf T}XA\in\mathbb S_+^m.\]
If additionally \(X\succ0\) and \(A\) has full column rank, then \(A^{\mathsf T}XA\succ0\). When \(m=n\) and \(A\) is invertible, the map \(X\mapsto A^{\mathsf T}XA\) is a bijection of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) onto itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Congruence maps preserve positive semidefiniteness, preserve positive definiteness under full-column-rank factors, and become PSD-cone bijections for invertible square factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A^{\mathsf T}XA\in\mathbb S_+^m\); if \(X\succ0\) and \(A\) has full column rank, then \(A^{\mathsf T}XA\succ0\).

notation.meaning: Congruence image of X under A.

children.title: Rank Preservation under Congruence
children.top_down_role: Rank-stratum behavior under invertible coordinate transformations.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(A^{\mathsf T}XA)=\operatorname{rank}(X)\).

notation.meaning: Real symmetric matrices of order n.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invertible real congruence of symmetric matrices.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.4 Positive definite matrices p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) and let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be invertible. Then
\[\operatorname{rank}(A^{\mathsf T}XA)=\operatorname{rank}(X),\qquad \ker(A^{\mathsf T}XA)=A^{-1}\ker(X).\]
Consequently, invertible congruence preserves the nullity and rank of every symmetric matrix. In particular, its restriction to \(\mathbb S_+^n\) maps each set \(\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{rank}(X)=r\}\) onto itself for every \(0\leq r\leq n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible congruence preserves rank and nullity, so each fixed-rank portion of the PSD cone is invariant.
knowledge_statements.title: Rank Preservation under Congruence

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.4 Positive definite matrices p. 20

children.title: PSD Cone Automorphism Orbits
children.top_down_role: Orbit structure induced by automorphisms of the positive-semidefinite cone.

knowledge_statements.title: PSD Cone Automorphism Orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orbit decomposition under invertible real congruence transformations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(A\in GL(n)\), let \(\Phi_A:\mathbb S_+^n\to\mathbb S_+^n\) be the congruence automorphism \(\Phi_A(X)=A^{\mathsf T}XA\). For each \(r\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), set \(D_r=\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0_{n-r})\). Then
\[\{\Phi_A(D_r):A\in GL(n)\}=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{rank}(X)=r\}.\]
Thus the orbits under invertible congruence are classified exactly by rank. The positive-definite cone is the orbit corresponding to \(r=n\), while each \(r<n\) gives a boundary orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The invertible-congruence orbits of the PSD cone are precisely its fixed-rank sets, with one orbit for each rank from zero to n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The orbit of \(D_r=\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0)\) under invertible congruence is exactly \(\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{rank}(X)=r\}\).

notation.meaning: General linear group of invertible real n-by-n matrices.

children.title: Positive-Definite Interior
children.top_down_role: Interior organization through positive-definite matrices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}(\mathbb S_+^n)=\mathbb S_{++}^n=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:\lambda_{\min}(X)>0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean interior inside the symmetric-matrix space.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.4 Positive definite matrices p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In the Euclidean space \(\mathbb S^n\), the interior of the positive-semidefinite cone is
\[\operatorname{int}(\mathbb S_+^n)=\mathbb S_{++}^n=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:x^{\mathsf T}Xx>0\text{ for every }x\neq0\}=\{X\in\mathbb S^n:\lambda_{\min}(X)>0\}.\]
Equivalently, \(X\in\operatorname{int}(\mathbb S_+^n)\) precisely when some \(\varepsilon>0\) satisfies \(X\succeq\varepsilon I_n\). Every such matrix has rank \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interior of the PSD cone is exactly the positive-definite cone, equivalently the matrices whose smallest eigenvalue is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Definite Interior

source_witnesses.locator: 2.3.4 Positive definite matrices p. 20

children.title: Singular PSD Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundary organization through singular positive-semidefinite matrices.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial\mathbb S_+^n=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\det X=0\}=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{rank}(X)<n\}\).

notation.meaning: Topological boundary in the symmetric-matrix space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean boundary of the finite-dimensional PSD cone.

source_refs.locator: 2.3.4 Positive definite matrices p. 20

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The boundary of the positive-semidefinite cone in \(\mathbb S^n\) is
\[\partial\mathbb S_+^n=\mathbb S_+^n\setminus\mathbb S_{++}^n=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\lambda_{\min}(X)=0\}.\]
For a positive-semidefinite matrix, this is equivalent to singularity, so
\[\partial\mathbb S_+^n=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\det X=0\}=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{rank}(X)<n\}.\]
Hence the boundary is the disjoint union of the fixed-rank sets with ranks \(0,1,\ldots,n-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PSD boundary consists exactly of singular PSD matrices, equivalently those with zero smallest eigenvalue or rank below n.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular PSD Boundary

children.title: Fixed-Rank Strata
children.top_down_role: Geometric layers indexed by matrix rank.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal S_r^+=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{rank}(X)=r\}\) is a smooth manifold of dimension \(nr-r(r-1)/2\).

notation.meaning: Rank-r stratum of the PSD cone.
Orthogonal group acting on factors from the right.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth real manifold structure of each PSD rank stratum.

source_refs.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(0\leq r\leq n\), define \(\mathcal S_r^+=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{rank}(X)=r\}\). For \(r>0\), the map \(U\mapsto UU^{\mathsf T}\) from the full-column-rank set \(\mathbb R_*^{n\times r}\) onto \(\mathcal S_r^+\) has fibers \(\{UQ:Q\in O(r)\}\). Consequently,
\[\mathcal S_r^+\cong\mathbb R_*^{n\times r}/O(r),\qquad \dim(\mathcal S_r^+)=nr-\frac{r(r-1)}2.\]
The case \(r=0\) is the zero-dimensional singleton \(\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each fixed-rank PSD set is a smooth stratum represented by full-rank rectangular factors modulo orthogonal transformations, with the stated dimension.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Rank Strata

children.title: Faces of the PSD Cone
children.top_down_role: Subspace- and rank-indexed facial organization.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) is a linear subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) is uniquely \(F_U=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{range}(X)\subseteq U\}\) for some subspace \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).

notation.meaning: Face indexed by the subspace U.
Orthogonal projector onto the indicated subspace.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete subspace-indexed classification of PSD-cone faces.

source_refs.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every linear subspace \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\),
\[F_U=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{range}(X)\subseteq U\}\]
is a face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\), and every face arises uniquely in this form. Moreover,
\[F_U=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\langle P_{U^\perp},X\rangle=0\},\]
so every PSD-cone face is exposed. If \(V\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) has full column rank and \(\operatorname{range}(V)=U\), then \(F_U=\{VSV^{\mathsf T}:S\in\mathbb S_+^k\}\), making the face linearly isomorphic to \(\mathbb S_+^k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every PSD-cone face is uniquely indexed by a subspace and contains precisely the PSD matrices whose ranges lie in that subspace.
knowledge_statements.title: Faces of the PSD Cone

source_witnesses.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subspace characterization of faces of the PSD cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the faces of the positive-semidefinite cone by their common range subspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\subseteq\mathcal S_+^n\). Then \(F\) is a face of \(\mathcal S_+^n\) if and only if there exists a linear subspace \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) such that \[F=\{X\in\mathcal S_+^n:\mathcal R(X)\subseteq L\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subset of the PSD cone is a face exactly when it consists of all PSD matrices whose ranges lie in one fixed subspace of R^n.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a face of }\mathcal S_+^n\iff\exists L\leq\mathbb R^n:\;F=\{X\in\mathcal S_+^n\mid\mathcal R(X)\subseteq L\}.

children.title: Minimal Faces of Affine Sections
children.top_down_role: Smallest cone faces carrying spectrahedral feasible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Faces of Affine Sections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal PSD face carrying a nonempty spectrahedral section.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb S^n\) be affine and let \(C=\mathcal A\cap\mathbb S_+^n\neq\varnothing\). Define
\[U=\operatorname{span}\{\operatorname{range}(X):X\in C\}.\]
Then the smallest face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) containing \(C\) is
\[\operatorname{face}_{\mathbb S_+^n}(C)=F_U=\{Z\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{range}(Z)\subseteq U\}.\]
Equivalently, its common kernel is \(U^\perp=\bigcap_{X\in C}\ker(X)\). If \(\bar X\in\operatorname{relint}(C)\), then \(U=\operatorname{range}(\bar X)\), so one relative-interior feasible matrix determines the minimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty affine PSD section lies in the face indexed by the span of all feasible ranges; any relative-interior feasible matrix identifies that face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The minimal face containing \(C\) is \(F_U\), where \(U=\operatorname{span}\{\operatorname{range}(X):X\in C\}\).

notation.meaning: Nonempty affine section of the PSD cone.
Span of ranges of all feasible matrices.

children.title: Exposed PSD Faces
children.top_down_role: Positive-semidefinite faces identified through supporting linear functionals.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed PSD Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization and exposure of every face of the finite-dimensional PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a linear subspace and let \(P_{L^\perp}\) denote the orthogonal projector onto \(L^\perp\). The associated face of the positive-semidefinite cone is
\[
F_L=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\operatorname{range}(X)\subseteq L\}=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\langle P_{L^\perp},X\rangle=0\}.
\]
Thus \(F_L\) is exposed by \(P_{L^\perp}\in\mathbb S_+^n\). Conversely, every face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) equals \(F_L\) for a unique subspace \(L\), namely the span of the ranges of its matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every PSD-cone face consists of matrices supported on one subspace and is exposed by the orthogonal projector onto that subspace’s complement.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb S^n\) carries the trace inner product \(\langle A,B\rangle=\operatorname{tr}(AB)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_L=\mathbb S_+^n\cap\{P_{L^\perp}\}^{\perp}\), and every face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) has this form.

notation.meaning: Cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices of order n.
Orthogonal projector onto the orthogonal complement of L.

children.title: Linear Images of the PSD Cone
children.top_down_role: Geometric behavior of positive-semidefinite cones under linear maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Images of the PSD Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear images, also called PSD-representable cones or homogeneous spectrahedral shadows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a linear map \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^m\), the linear image of the PSD cone is
\[
\mathcal A(\mathbb S_+^n)=\{\mathcal A(X):X\in\mathbb S_+^n\}.
\]
It is a convex cone and admits the lifted representation \(y\in\mathcal A(\mathbb S_+^n)\) if and only if there exists \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\) satisfying \(\mathcal A(X)=y\). Despite being the image of a closed convex cone, \(\mathcal A(\mathbb S_+^n)\) need not be closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear PSD image comprises all vectors obtained by applying a linear map to PSD matrices; it is convex but may fail to be closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A(\mathbb S_+^n)\) is a convex cone with an existential PSD lift, but closedness is not automatic.

notation.meaning: Linear map from symmetric matrices to a finite-dimensional vector space.
Cone of real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrices.

children.title: Projection Closure Failures
children.top_down_role: Nonclosed image phenomena relevant to semidefinite representations and duality.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Closure Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal nonclosed projection of a two-by-two PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(\pi:\mathbb S^2\to\mathbb R^2\) by \(\pi\!\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x&y\\y&z\end{smallmatrix}\right)=(x,y)\). Then
\[
\pi(\mathbb S_+^2)=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.
\]
Consequently, \((1/k,1)\in\pi(\mathbb S_+^2)\) for every positive integer \(k\), whereas its limit \((0,1)\notin\pi(\mathbb S_+^2)\). Thus \(\pi(\mathbb S_+^2)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting a two-by-two PSD matrix onto its first diagonal and off-diagonal entries produces a convex cone that is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi(\mathbb S_+^2)\) is not closed, and \(\overline{\pi(\mathbb S_+^2)}=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x\geq0\}\).

notation.meaning: Specified coordinate projection from two-by-two symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Tangent Cones at PSD Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bouligand tangent cone of the finite-dimensional PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\), and let the columns of \(U_0\) form an orthonormal basis for \(\ker X\). The Bouligand tangent cone to \(\mathbb S_+^n\) at \(X\) is
\[
T_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)=\{H\in\mathbb S^n:U_0^{\mathsf T}HU_0\succeq0\}.
\]
Equivalently, a symmetric direction is tangent precisely when its compression to the nullspace of \(X\) is positive semidefinite; its remaining blocks in an eigenbasis of \(X\) are unrestricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric direction is tangent to the PSD cone exactly when its restriction to the kernel of the base matrix is PSD.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)=\{H:U_0^{\mathsf T}HU_0\succeq0\}\).

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone to C at X.
Orthonormal basis matrix for the kernel of X.

children.title: Normal Cones at PSD Points

knowledge_statements.title: Normal Cones at PSD Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-analytic normal cone using the outward-normal sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\), define the normal cone by \(N_C(X)=\{Y:\langle Y,Z-X\rangle\leq0\text{ for every }Z\in C\}\). Then
\[
N_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)=\{Y\in\mathbb S^n:Y\preceq0,\ \langle Y,X\rangle=0\}=\{Y\in\mathbb S^n:Y\preceq0,\ YX=0\}.
\]
Thus every normal is negative semidefinite and supported on \(\ker X\). Under the opposite conic-dual sign convention, the corresponding multiplier is \(-Y\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With the outward-normal convention, PSD-cone normals are negative semidefinite matrices complementary to the base point and supported on its kernel.
assumptions_latex: The trace inner product and outward-normal convention are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)=(-\mathbb S_+^n)\cap\{X\}^{\perp}\).

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic outward normal cone to C at X.
Trace inner product on symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Critical Cones for SDP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical cone for a PSD constraint and a complementary outward normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(Y\in N_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)\). The critical cone of the PSD constraint at \(X\) relative to \(Y\) is
\[
K(X,Y)=T_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)\cap Y^\perp
      =\{H\in\mathbb S^n:U_0^{\mathsf T}HU_0\succeq0,\ \langle Y,H\rangle=0\},
\]
where \(U_0\) spans \(\ker X\). It consists of first-order PSD-feasible directions on which the active normal has zero first-order pairing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The SDP critical cone comprises tangent directions orthogonal to a complementary normal, capturing first-order feasible directions with zero normal pairing.
assumptions_latex: \(Y\in N_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)\) under the outward-normal convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(X,Y)=T_{\mathbb S_+^n}(X)\cap\{H:\langle Y,H\rangle=0\}\).

notation.meaning: Critical cone at X relative to normal Y.
Orthonormal basis matrix for the kernel of X.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical Cone for a Nonlinear Semidefinite Constraint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-cone and multiplier representations of critical directions in nonlinear semidefinite optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At the reference point \(\bar x\), with \(\bar y=G(\bar x)\in K\), the critical cone is
\[
C(\bar x)=\{h\in\mathbb R^n:DG(\bar x)h\in T_K(\bar y),\;Df(\bar x)h=0\}.
\]
If \(\Lambda(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\), then for every \(\Omega\in\Lambda(\bar x)\),
\[
C(\bar x)=\{h\in\mathbb R^n:DG(\bar x)h\in T_K(\bar y),\;\Omega\bullet DG(\bar x)h=0\}.
\]
The critical cone is closed and convex; under multiplier existence, it is also the set of optimal solutions of the corresponding linearized problem, whose optimal value is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The nonlinear-SDP critical cone consists of tangent linearized directions with zero first-order objective variation. When multipliers exist, it has an equivalent multiplier-orthogonality representation and equals the solution set of the zero-valued linearized problem. It is a closed convex cone.
assumptions_latex: \Lambda(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\text{ for the multiplier and linearized-problem characterizations}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C(\bar x)=\{h:DG(\bar x)h\in T_K(\bar y),\ Df(\bar x)h=0\};\quad \Lambda(\bar x)\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow C(\bar x)=\{h:DG(\bar x)h\in T_K(\bar y),\ \Omega\bullet DG(\bar x)h=0\}\text{ for every }\Omega\in\Lambda(\bar x),\text{ and }C(\bar x)\text{ is closed and convex}.

children.title: Definite-Pivot Schur Complements
children.top_down_role: Classical block positivity under nonsingular positive pivots.

knowledge_statements.title: Definite-Pivot Schur Complements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical block-positivity equivalence with a positive-definite leading pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb S^p\), \(C\in\mathbb S^q\), and \(B\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\), with \(A\succ0\). Then
\[
\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^{\mathsf T}&C\end{pmatrix}\succeq0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
C-B^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}B\succeq0.
\]
Moreover, replacing both non-strict inequalities by strict inequalities gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^{\mathsf T}&C\end{pmatrix}\succ0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
C-B^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}B\succ0.
\]
The analogous equivalence holds after pivoting on \(C\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a positive-definite pivot, block-matrix positivity is equivalent to positivity of the ordinary Schur complement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^{\mathsf T}&C\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\iff C-B^{\mathsf T}A^{-1}B\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: Schur complement of A in the block matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb S^n\), \(B\in\mathbb S^m\), \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), and \(B\succ0\). For \(M=\begin{bmatrix}A&X\\X^\top&B\end{bmatrix}\) and \(S=A-XB^{-1}X^\top\), one has \(M\succeq0\iff S\succeq0\) and \(M\succ0\iff S\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With a positive-definite lower-right pivot B, a symmetric block matrix is positive semidefinite or positive definite exactly when A minus X B inverse X transpose has the corresponding property.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\succeq0\iff S\succeq0,\qquad M\succ0\iff S\succ0

children.title: Singular-Pivot Range Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Range-sensitive compatibility regimes for block positivity with singular pivot blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Pivot Range Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition required when a Schur-complement pivot is singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb S_+^p\) and \(B\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\). Range compatibility of the possibly singular pivot \(A\) with \(B\) is
\[
\operatorname{range}(B)\subseteq\operatorname{range}(A).
\]
Equivalently,
\[
(I-AA^\dagger)B=0,
\]
where \(A^\dagger\) is the Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse. If there exists \(C\in\mathbb S^q\) such that
\[
\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^{\mathsf T}&C\end{pmatrix}\succeq0,
\]
then this range-compatibility condition is necessary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a possibly singular PSD pivot, every column of the coupling block must lie in the pivot's range; this condition is necessary for a positive-semidefinite block completion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{range}(B)\subseteq\operatorname{range}(A)\iff(I-AA^\dagger)B=0\), and this condition is necessary for the existence of \(C\in\mathbb S^q\) making the block matrix positive semidefinite.

children.title: Generalized Schur Complements
children.top_down_role: Pseudoinverse-based complement structures for singular block matrices.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Schur Complements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-semidefinite block criterion with a possibly singular leading pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb S^p\), \(C\in\mathbb S^q\), and \(B\in\mathbb R^{p\times q}\). Then
\[
\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^{\mathsf T}&C\end{pmatrix}\succeq0
\]
if and only if all three conditions hold:
\[
A\succeq0,\qquad (I-AA^\dagger)B=0,\qquad C-B^{\mathsf T}A^\dagger B\succeq0.
\]
Equivalently, the range condition is \(\operatorname{range}(B)\subseteq\operatorname{range}(A)\). A symmetric criterion follows by pivoting on \(C\) instead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block matrix with singular PSD pivot is PSD exactly when range compatibility holds and the pseudoinverse Schur complement is PSD.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^{\mathsf T}&C\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\iff A\succeq0,\ (I-AA^\dagger)B=0,\ C-B^{\mathsf T}A^\dagger B\succeq0\).

children.title: Degenerate Block-Positivity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Boundary cases where ordinary definite-pivot reductions cease to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Block-Positivity Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a pseudoinverse Schur test when range compatibility is omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For scalars \(b,c\), consider
\[
M(b,c)=\begin{pmatrix}0&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The pivot \(A=0\) is PSD and has pseudoinverse \(A^\dagger=0\), so the generalized Schur expression equals \(c\). Nevertheless,
\[
M(b,c)\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad b=0\ \text{ and }\ c\geq0.
\]
Thus \(c\geq0\) alone is insufficient: any \(b\neq0\) violates the required compatibility \(\operatorname{range}(b)\subseteq\operatorname{range}(0)=\{0\}\) and makes the block matrix indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a zero pivot, a nonzero coupling makes the block matrix indefinite even when the pseudoinverse Schur expression is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(b\neq0\) and \(c\geq0\), the pseudoinverse Schur inequality holds while \(M(b,c)\not\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: Two-by-two symmetric block matrix with zero leading pivot.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Epigraph Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Schur-complement LMI representation of a convex quadratic epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\geq1\), \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(t\in\mathbb R\). Then
\[
t\geq x^{\mathsf T}Qx
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\begin{pmatrix}t&x^{\mathsf T}Q^{1/2}\\Q^{1/2}x&I_n\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
\]
More generally, for \(d\geq1\), \(F\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\), \(z\in\mathbb R^d\), and \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), the substitution \(x=Fz+g\) yields an LMI representation of
\[
t\geq(Fz+g)^{\mathsf T}Q(Fz+g).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a PSD quadratic form, including one composed with an affine map, has an exact block-LMI representation.
assumptions_latex: \(Q^{1/2}\) is the symmetric PSD square root of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:t\geq x^{\mathsf T}Qx\}=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\begin{pmatrix}t&x^{\mathsf T}Q^{1/2}\\Q^{1/2}x&I_n\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\}\).

notation.meaning: Symmetric positive-semidefinite square root of Q.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Ball LMI Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard block-LMI representation of the Euclidean norm cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\geq1\), \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(t\in\mathbb R\). Then
\[
\lVert x\rVert_2\leq t
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\begin{pmatrix}t&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&tI_n\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.
\]
For every fixed \(r\geq0\), the closed Euclidean ball has the representation
\[
\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\lVert x\rVert_2\leq r\}
=
\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\begin{pmatrix}r&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&rI_n\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Euclidean norm cone and every fixed-radius Euclidean ball have exact symmetric block-LMI representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\lVert x\rVert_2\leq t\}=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R:\begin{pmatrix}t&x^{\mathsf T}\\x&tI_n\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-Inverse Epigraph Lifts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator epigraph of matrix inversion under the Loewner order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\in\mathbb S_{++}^{n}\) and \(Y\in\mathbb S^{n}\), the matrix-inverse epigraph has the LMI representation
\[\{(X,Y):Y\succeq X^{-1}\}=\left\{(X,Y):\begin{bmatrix}X&I_n\\ I_n&Y\end{bmatrix}\succeq0\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a real symmetric positive-definite matrix X, the condition that Y is a Loewner upper bound on the inverse of X is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of the displayed block matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y\succeq X^{-1}\iff \begin{bmatrix}X&I_n\\ I_n&Y\end{bmatrix}\succeq0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar-Variable Matrix Pencils
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric affine pencils in finitely many scalar variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given fixed matrices \(A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\), a scalar-variable affine matrix pencil is the map
\[L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb S^n,\qquad L(x)=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_iA_i.\]
Its positive-semidefinite feasible set
\[S_L=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:L(x)\succeq0\}\]
is a closed convex spectrahedron, which may be empty or unbounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar-variable matrix pencil is an affine symmetric matrix expression. Requiring it to be positive semidefinite defines a closed convex spectrahedron, possibly empty or unbounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\mathbb R^m:A_0+\sum_{i=1}^m x_iA_i\succeq0\}\) is a spectrahedron.

notation.meaning: space of real symmetric matrices of order n

knowledge_statements.title: Structured Matrix-Variable Pencils
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine pencils over finite-dimensional matrix-variable spaces with prescribed symmetry, block structure, or sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space of structured matrix variables, let \(A_0\in\mathbb S^n\), and let \(\mathcal A:V\to\mathbb S^n\) be linear. The associated structured matrix-variable pencil is
\[L(X)=A_0+\mathcal A(X),\qquad X\in V.\]
For a basis \(E_1,\ldots,E_m\) of \(V\) and coordinates \(X=\sum_{j=1}^m x_jE_j\), the pencil has the scalar-coordinate form
\[L(X)=A_0+\sum_{j=1}^m x_j\mathcal A(E_j).\]
Thus \(\{X\in V:L(X)\succeq0\}\) is spectrahedral in coordinates on \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A structured matrix-variable pencil is an affine linear map on a finite-dimensional structured matrix space. Choosing a basis expresses its semidefinite constraint as an ordinary scalar-variable LMI.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space of structured matrix variables
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{X\in V:A_0+\mathcal A(X)\succeq0\}\) is a spectrahedral feasible set in coordinates on \(V\).

notation.meaning: linear map from structured variables to symmetric matrices

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Spectrahedral Sections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of spectrahedra under affine inverse images and parameterized affine sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:L(x)\succeq0\}\), where \(L\) is an affine symmetric pencil, and let \(T:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^m\) be affine. Then
\[T^{-1}(S)=\{y\in\mathbb R^k:L(T(y))\succeq0\}\]
is a spectrahedron. If \(T\) is surjective onto an affine subspace \(H\subseteq\mathbb R^m\), then
\[T\bigl(T^{-1}(S)\bigr)=S\cap H.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse image of a spectrahedron under an affine map is a spectrahedron. When the map parameterizes an affine subspace H surjectively, the image of that inverse image is the section of the original spectrahedron by H.
assumptions_latex: \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:L(x)\succeq0\}\) for an affine symmetric pencil \(L\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T^{-1}(S)=\{y\in\mathbb R^k:L(T(y))\succeq0\}\) is a spectrahedron.

notation.meaning: affine map used to parameterize a section
inverse image of S under T

children.title: Coordinate Slices of Spectrahedra
children.top_down_role: Restricted spectrahedral families obtained by fixing selected coordinates.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The free-coordinate parameterization of \(S\cap\{x:x_j=c_j\text{ for }j\in J\}\) is a spectrahedron.

notation.meaning: affine symmetric pencil defining the original spectrahedron

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slices obtained by fixing selected scalar coordinates.

source_refs.locator: 1.4.1 Affine sections of psd cones p. 19

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L(x)=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^m x_iA_i\) and \(S=\{x:L(x)\succeq0\}\). Fix coordinates \(x_j=c_j\) for \(j\in J\), and let \(K=\{1,\ldots,m\}\setminus J\). In the free coordinates \(z=(z_i)_{i\in K}\), the slice is represented by
\[\left\{z:\left(A_0+\sum_{j\in J}c_jA_j\right)+\sum_{i\in K}z_iA_i\succeq0\right\}.\]
Thus every coordinate slice of a spectrahedron is a spectrahedron, including empty slices and lower-dimensional slices meeting only the boundary of the original set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing any subset of a spectrahedron's coordinates yields a new affine matrix pencil in the remaining coordinates, hence another spectrahedron.

children.title: Product-Cone Spectrahedra
children.top_down_role: Multiple semidefinite constraints represented through product or block structure.

assumptions_latex: Each \(L_r\) is an affine symmetric pencil
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\prod_{r=1}^q S_r=\{(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(q)}):\operatorname{diag}(L_1(x^{(1)}),\ldots,L_q(x^{(q)}))\succeq0\}\).

source_refs.locator: 5.5 Spectrahedra and Semidefinite Programming p. 231

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(r=1,\ldots,q\), let \(S_r=\{x^{(r)}:L_r(x^{(r)})\succeq0\}\), where each \(L_r\) is an affine symmetric pencil. Their Cartesian product has the single-pencil representation
\[\prod_{r=1}^q S_r=\left\{(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(q)}):\operatorname{diag}\bigl(L_1(x^{(1)}),\ldots,L_q(x^{(q)})\bigr)\succeq0\right\}.\]
A block-diagonal symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when every diagonal block is positive semidefinite. Consequently, finite products and finite intersections of LMI constraints can be encoded by one block-diagonal LMI.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite product of spectrahedra is represented by placing their defining pencils on the diagonal of one block matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine LMIs and basic Schur-complement representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strict and nonstrict affine LMIs and records convexity, block-diagonal aggregation, and exact Schur-complement representations of several convex constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F(x)=F_0+\sum_{i=1}^m x_iF_i, where x\in\mathbb R^m and F_i=F_i^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}. The strict LMI F(x)\succ0 means u^TF(x)u>0 for every nonzero u\in\mathbb R^n; equivalently, all leading principal minors of F(x) are positive. Its nonstrict analogue is F(x)\succeq0. The set \{x:F(x)\succ0\} is convex. A finite family F^{(j)}(x)\succ0 is equivalent to \operatorname{diag}(F^{(1)}(x),\ldots,F^{(p)}(x))\succ0, and a diagonal LMI is a system of linear inequalities. For affine Q(x)=Q(x)^T, R(x)=R(x)^T, and S(x), \begin{bmatrix}Q(x)&S(x)\\S(x)^T&R(x)\end{bmatrix}\succ0 \iff R(x)\succ0\ \text{and}\ Q(x)-S(x)R(x)^{-1}S(x)^T\succ0. Consequently, \|Z(x)\|_2<1 \iff \begin{bmatrix}I&Z(x)\\Z(x)^T&I\end{bmatrix}\succ0. If P(x)=P(x)^T and c(x) are affine, then P(x)\succ0 and c(x)^TP(x)^{-1}c(x)<1 \iff \begin{bmatrix}P(x)&c(x)\\c(x)^T&1\end{bmatrix}\succ0. More generally, P(x)\succ0 and \operatorname{Tr}(S(x)^TP(x)^{-1}S(x))<1 hold iff there exists X=X^T such that \operatorname{Tr}X<1 and \begin{bmatrix}X&S(x)^T\\S(x)&P(x)\end{bmatrix}\succ0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine symmetric matrix inequality is strict when its matrix is positive definite and nonstrict when it is positive semidefinite. The strict feasible set is convex. Several LMIs can be combined block-diagonally, and diagonal LMIs reduce to linear inequalities. Schur complements give exact LMI representations of spectral-norm, inverse-quadratic, and trace inverse-quadratic constraints, with a symmetric slack matrix in the trace case.
assumptions_latex: Q(x)=Q(x)^T,\quad R(x)=R(x)^T,\quad S(x)\text{ are affine and dimensionally compatible}
Z(x),\ c(x),\ P(x)=P(x)^T,\ S(x)\text{ are affine with the displayed compatible dimensions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:F(x)\succ0\}\text{ is convex, and the displayed block-diagonal and Schur-complement equivalences provide exact LMI representations under their stated definiteness assumptions.}

children.title: Strict LMI Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Interior feasibility and strict-inequality normalization regimes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict feasibility holds exactly when \(\exists x\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(L(x)\succ0\), equivalently \(\exists x,\epsilon>0\) with \(L(x)\succeq\epsilon I_n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strict feasibility for an affine symmetric pencil.

source_refs.locator: 2.5 Strict and Nonstrict LMIs p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an affine symmetric pencil \(L(x)=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^m x_iA_i\), the LMI is strictly feasible when
\[\exists x\in\mathbb R^m\quad L(x)\succ0.\]
In finite dimensions this is equivalent to the margin form
\[\exists x\in\mathbb R^m,\ \exists\epsilon>0\quad L(x)\succeq\epsilon I_n,\]
and also to \(\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^m}\lambda_{\min}(L(x))>0\). Any strictly feasible matrix lies in the interior of the positive-semidefinite cone; accordingly, its smallest eigenvalue supplies a positive strict-feasibility margin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LMI is strictly feasible when some pencil value is positive definite, equivalently when it dominates a positive multiple of the identity.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict LMI Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict feasibility of an LMI
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines strict feasibility for a symmetric LMI and identifies it as a strong constraint qualification. The context-dependent EVP, GEVP, and CP consequence is excluded because those formulations are not specified in this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{S}^n\) be an affine symmetric matrix function. The LMI \(F(x)\succeq 0\) is strictly feasible if its strict version is feasible; equivalently, if there exists \(x_0\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(F(x_0)\succ 0\). This strict-feasibility requirement is a strong constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An LMI is strictly feasible when some parameter value makes its matrix positive definite. This requirement is a strong constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(x)\succeq0\text{ is strictly feasible}\iff\exists x_0\in\mathbb{R}^m\text{ such that }F(x_0)\succ0.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonstrict feasibility holds exactly when \(\exists x\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(L(x)\succeq0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an affine symmetric pencil \(L(x)=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^m x_iA_i\), the nonstrict LMI feasibility condition is
\[\exists x\in\mathbb R^m	ext{ such that }L(x)\succeq0.\]
Equivalently, every eigenvalue of \(L(x)\) is nonnegative, or \(\lambda_{\min}(L(x))\geq0\). Feasibility permits singular matrices and therefore includes points on the boundary of the positive-semidefinite cone. It does not imply strict feasibility: the entire feasible image may lie in a proper face of that cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonstrict LMI is feasible when some pencil value is positive semidefinite; the feasible value may be singular and confined to the cone boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonstrict LMI Feasibility

knowledge_statements.title: Homogeneous LMI Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scale invariance and valid normalization of homogeneous LMI solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L(x)=\sum_{i=1}^m x_iA_i\) with \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\). The feasible set
\[K=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:L(x)\succeq0\}\]
is a closed convex cone and satisfies \(L(\alpha x)=\alpha L(x)\) for every \(\alpha\geq0\). A nonzero feasible ray can be normalized by \(c^{\mathsf T}x=1\) when it contains a representative \(x\) satisfying \(c^{\mathsf T}x>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A homogeneous LMI has a closed convex feasible cone invariant under nonnegative scaling. A linear equality can normalize a nonzero feasible ray when the normalizing functional is positive on that ray.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(\alpha x)=\alpha L(x)\) for \(\alpha\geq0\), and \(\{x\in\mathbb R^m:L(x)\succeq0\}\) is a convex cone.

children.title: Generalized-Eigenvalue LMI Problems
children.top_down_role: Parameterized quasiconvex models organized through repeated LMI feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Eigenvalue LMI Problems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quasiconvex generalized-eigenvalue minimization solved through parameterized LMI feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[t_\star=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:\exists x\in C\text{ such that }A(x)-tB(x)\preceq0\},\]
where \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is convex, \(A\) and \(B\) are affine symmetric matrix pencils, and \(B(x)\succ0\) for every \(x\in C\). Suppose \(\ell<u\), the level \(\ell\) is infeasible, the level \(u\) is feasible with a retained feasible point, and \(\varepsilon>0\). At each iteration set \(t=(\ell+u)/2\) and test feasibility of
\[x\in C,\qquad A(x)-tB(x)\preceq0.\]
Replace \(u\) by \(t\) and retain the feasible point when the test is feasible; otherwise replace \(\ell\) by \(t\). When \(u-\ell\leq\varepsilon\), the interval \([\ell,u]\) brackets \(t_\star\), and \(u\) has a retained feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given an infeasible lower level and a feasible upper level, bisection repeatedly solves the fixed-level convex LMI feasibility problem. It terminates with an interval of prescribed width that brackets the optimal generalized-eigenvalue level and with a feasible upper endpoint.
assumptions_latex: \(A(x)\) and \(B(x)\) are affine symmetric matrix pencils
For each fixed \(t\), membership in \(C\) together with \(A(x)-tB(x)\preceq0\) is a convex feasibility problem
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bisection produces \(\ell\leq t_\star\leq u\) with \(u-\ell\leq\varepsilon\), and the final upper endpoint \(u\) is feasible.

notation.meaning: current infeasible lower and feasible upper endpoints

children.title: Congruence Transformations
children.top_down_role: Positivity-preserving transformations of LMI matrix expressions.

knowledge_statements.title: Congruence Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of semidefinite and definite order under nonsingular congruence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(X\in\mathbb S^n\) and nonsingular \(P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), congruence preserves positive semidefiniteness and positive definiteness:
\[X\succeq0\iff P^{\mathsf T}XP\succeq0,\qquad X\succ0\iff P^{\mathsf T}XP\succ0.\]
Consequently, for any symmetric pencil \(L(x)\), the constraints \(L(x)\succeq0\) and \(P^{\mathsf T}L(x)P\succeq0\) have the same feasible set, with strict feasibility preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular congruence transformation preserves positive semidefiniteness and positive definiteness. Applying a fixed nonsingular congruence to an LMI therefore preserves its feasible set and strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X\succeq0\iff P^{\mathsf T}XP\succeq0\), and \(X\succ0\iff P^{\mathsf T}XP\succ0\).

children.title: Orthogonal Basis Changes
children.top_down_role: Basis changes preserving spectral and semidefinite structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Orthogonal Basis Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral invariance of symmetric pencils under orthogonal changes of basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) satisfy \(Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_n\). For every \(X\in\mathbb S^n\), the matrices \(Q^{\mathsf T}XQ\) and \(X\) have the same eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity:
\[\lambda_i(Q^{\mathsf T}XQ)=\lambda_i(X),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.\]
Consequently, an orthogonal basis change preserves positive semidefiniteness, positive definiteness, rank, determinant, and the smallest-eigenvalue margin. Applied to a symmetric pencil \(L(x)\), it preserves the LMI feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthogonal basis change preserves all eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix and therefore preserves semidefinite order, rank, determinant, minimum-eigenvalue margins, and the feasible set of a transformed LMI.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q^{\mathsf T}XQ\) has the same eigenvalues as \(X\), hence preserves semidefinite order and spectral margins.

children.title: Coordinate-Scaling Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Diagonal and structured scalings used to obtain equivalent LMI descriptions.

assumptions_latex: \(F(x)=F_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_i\in\mathbb S^m\) is an affine symmetric pencil on \(\mathbb R^n\).
\(D\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is diagonal and nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)\succeq0\iff DF(x)D\succeq0\); under \(x=Tz\), the feasible set in \(z\) is \(T^{-1}\{x\in\mathbb R^n:F(x)\succeq0\}\).

notation.meaning: Nonsingular linear scaling of the decision coordinates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diagonal congruence scaling preserves the feasible set in the same decision coordinates; an invertible decision-variable scaling gives an equivalent reparametrization. No equivalence under singular scaling is asserted.

source_refs.locator: 2.1 From Linear to Semidefinite Optimization p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=F_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_i\in\mathbb S^m\), let \(D\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) be diagonal and nonsingular, and let \(T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular. Then
\[
F(x)\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad DF(x)D\succeq0.
\]
Consequently, replacing each coefficient \(F_i\) by \(DF_iD\) preserves the feasible set in \(x\). Under the coordinate substitution \(x=Tz\), the transformed LMI \(DF(Tz)D\succeq0\) has feasible set
\[
T^{-1}\{x\in\mathbb R^n:F(x)\succeq0\}
\]
in the \(z\)-coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular diagonal congruence preserves an LMI's feasible decision vectors. A nonsingular scaling of the decision variables instead gives an equivalent coordinate reparametrization, whose feasible set is the inverse image of the original set.
knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate-Scaling Equivalence

children.title: Block-Diagonal Aggregation
children.top_down_role: Combination of multiple semidefinite constraints into a block-diagonal constraint.

assumptions_latex: \(k\ge1\), and for \(j=1,\ldots,k\), \(F_j(x)\in\mathbb S^{m_j}\) is an affine symmetric pencil on a common finite-dimensional decision space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_j(x)\succeq0\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,k\) if and only if \(\operatorname{diag}(F_1(x),\ldots,F_k(x))\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: Block-diagonal matrix with the listed diagonal blocks.
Cone of real positive semidefinite matrices of order \(m\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite aggregation of affine PSD constraints into one block-diagonal LMI.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Semidefinite programming p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(k\ge1\) and affine symmetric pencils \(F_j(x)\in\mathbb S^{m_j}\), define
\[
F(x)=\operatorname{diag}\bigl(F_1(x),\ldots,F_k(x)\bigr)\in\mathbb S^{m_1+\cdots+m_k}.
\]
Then
\[
F(x)\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_j(x)\succeq0\ \text{for every }j=1,\ldots,k.
\]
Thus a finite conjunction of LMI constraints is represented exactly by one block-diagonal LMI, without projection variables or a change to the feasible decision vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite collection of PSD constraints on common decision variables can be aggregated exactly into one block-diagonal PSD constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Block-Diagonal Aggregation

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1 Semidefinite programming p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Block-diagonal aggregation of finitely many LMIs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact aggregation of a finite LMI system; no equivalence is asserted for infinite constraint families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), let \(\mathcal A_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbf S^{m_i}\) be linear, and let \(B_i\in\mathbf S^{m_i}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\). Define \(\mathcal A x=\operatorname{Diag}(\mathcal A_1x,\ldots,\mathcal A_kx)\) and \(B=\operatorname{Diag}(B_1,\ldots,B_k)\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\mathcal A_i x-B_i\succeq0\) for all \(i=1,\ldots,k\) if and only if \(\mathcal A x-B\succeq0\), because a symmetric block-diagonal matrix is positive semidefinite if and only if each diagonal block is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any finite system of linear matrix inequalities is equivalent to one linear matrix inequality obtained by placing the individual matrix expressions along the diagonal of a block-diagonal matrix. This follows from the blockwise characterization of positive semidefiniteness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\mathbb R^n,\quad \left(\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,k\},\ \mathcal A_i x-B_i\succeq0\right)\iff\operatorname{Diag}(\mathcal A_1x-B_1,\ldots,\mathcal A_kx-B_k)\succeq0.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\succeq0\iff M_j\succeq0\) for every \(j=1,\ldots,k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise characterization of positive semidefiniteness for a finite block-diagonal matrix.

source_refs.locator: 1.1 Semidefinite programming p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(k\ge1\) and
\[
M=\operatorname{diag}(M_1,\ldots,M_k),
\]
where \(M_j\in\mathbb S^{m_j}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,k\). Then
\[
M\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad M_j\succeq0\ \text{for every }j=1,\ldots,k.
\]
Accordingly, a block-diagonal PSD constraint separates exactly into its individual PSD block constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite block-diagonal symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when every diagonal block is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.title: PSD Block Separation

children.title: Product-Cone Conversion
children.top_down_role: Equivalence between block semidefinite structure and explicit product-cone structure.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The map \((X_1,\ldots,X_k)\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(X_1,\ldots,X_k)\) identifies \(\prod_{j=1}^k\mathbb S_+^{m_j}\) with the corresponding block-diagonal subcone of \(\mathbb S_+^{m_1+\cdots+m_k}\).

notation.meaning: Cartesian product of the indicated PSD cones.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear cone identification between a finite product of PSD cones and the corresponding block-diagonal PSD subcone; the image is not asserted to be a face of the full PSD cone.

source_refs.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(k\ge1\) and let \(m_1,\ldots,m_k\) be positive integers. Define
\[
\Phi:\prod_{j=1}^k\mathbb S^{m_j}\to\mathbb S^{m_1+cdots+m_k},\qquad
\Phi(X_1,\ldots,X_k)=\operatorname{diag}(X_1,\ldots,X_k).
\]
The restriction of \(\Phi\) is a linear cone isomorphism from \(\prod_{j=1}^k\mathbb S_+^{m_j}\) onto
\[
\{X\in\mathbb S_+^{m_1+\cdots+m_k}:X\text{ is block diagonal with block sizes }m_1,\ldots,m_k\}.
\]
Therefore a constraint in the product cone converts exactly into one PSD constraint together with the prescribed block-zero linear equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite product of PSD cones is linearly isomorphic to the subcone of PSD matrices with the corresponding block-diagonal pattern.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Cone Conversion

children.title: Slack-Variable Lifts
children.top_down_role: Extended formulations using slack matrices or slack scalars.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)\succeq0\iff\exists S\in\mathbb S_+^m\) such that \(F(x)-S=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form lift of an affine PSD inequality using a matrix slack.

source_refs.locator: 2 Semidefinite Optimization p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an affine symmetric pencil \(F(x)\), the LMI feasible set has the lifted equality representation
\[
\{x:F(x)\succeq0\}
=
\{x:\exists S\in\mathbb S_+^m\text{ with }F(x)-S=0\}.
\]
The lifted formulation introduces a symmetric slack variable \(S\), constrains it to the PSD cone, and replaces the matrix inequality by an affine matrix equality. Eliminating \(S\) recovers the original LMI exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine PSD inequality is equivalent to an affine matrix equality with a positive semidefinite slack matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Slack-Variable Lifts

children.title: Auxiliary-Variable Extensions
children.top_down_role: Additional variables used to simplify affine matrix structure.

assumptions_latex: \(L(x,y)=L_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iL_i+\sum_{j=1}^p y_jM_j\in\mathbb S^m\) is affine and symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\{x:\exists y, L(x,y)\succeq0\}\) is the projection of a spectrahedron and hence is semidefinite representable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General finite-dimensional auxiliary-variable LMI extension and its projection.

source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L(x,y)=L_0+\sum_{i=1}^n x_iL_i+\sum_{j=1}^p y_jM_j\) be an affine symmetric pencil. The set represented by its auxiliary-variable extension is
\[
C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^p, L(x,y)\succeq0\}.
\]
Thus \(C\) is the coordinate projection of the spectrahedron \(\widehat C=\{(x,y):L(x,y)\succeq0\}\). The extension is exact for a target set \(C_0\) precisely when every \(x\in C_0\) admits such a \(y\), and no \(x\notin C_0\) does.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary variables extend an LMI in a higher-dimensional space; projecting its feasible set gives the represented set in the original variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Extensions

children.title: Epigraph LMI Lifts
children.top_down_role: Extended semidefinite representations of convex objective epigraphs.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper and convex.
\(L(x,t,y)\in\mathbb S^m\) is an affine symmetric pencil.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lift is exact when \(f(x)\le t\iff\exists y,L(x,t,y)\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projected-LMI representation of a convex function's epigraph.

source_refs.locator: 6.4 Constructing Semidefinite Representations p. 271
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An epigraph LMI lift of \(f\) is an affine symmetric pencil \(L(x,t,y)\) satisfying
\[
\operatorname{epi}f
=
\{(x,t)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}:\exists y\in\mathbb R^p, L(x,t,y)\succeq0\}.
\]
Equivalently, for every \((x,t)\),
\[
f(x)\le t\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y\in\mathbb R^p, L(x,t,y)\succeq0.
\]
Minimizing \(f(x)\) over additional constraints can then be replaced exactly by minimizing \(t\) subject to this lifted LMI and those constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epigraph LMI lift represents the inequality f(x) ≤ t as the projection of an affine positive semidefinite constraint.
knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph LMI Lifts

children.title: Variable Elimination
children.top_down_role: Removal of selected variables from affine matrix descriptions.

assumptions_latex: \(y\in\mathbb R^p\) consists of variables to be eliminated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eliminating \(y\) yields exactly \(C=\{x:\exists y,L(x,y)\succeq0\}\), which is semidefinite representable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential elimination of variables from one finite-dimensional affine LMI.

source_refs.locator: 6 Semidefinite Representability p. 251

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the spectrahedron
\[
\widehat C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^p:L(x,y)\succeq0\},
\]
elimination of \(y\) means forming
\[
C=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^p, L(x,y)\succeq0\}.
\]
This operation preserves convexity and produces a semidefinite-representable set. It need not produce a direct LMI in \(x\) alone; such a direct pencil exists only when the projected set is itself spectrahedral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating selected LMI variables means existentially projecting them out; the result remains semidefinite representable but may lack a direct LMI.
