children.title: Ordinary Farkas Certificates
children.top_down_role: Standard conic-alternative certificates for strongly infeasible SDP systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Farkas Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual PSD certificates for strong infeasibility of semidefinite equality systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the feasibility problem
\[\text{find }X\in\mathbb S_+^n\quad\text{such that}\quad \mathcal A(X)=b,\]
where \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is linear and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\). A vector \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying
\[\mathcal A^*y\succeq0,\qquad \langle b,y\rangle<0\]
is an ordinary Farkas certificate of infeasibility. Existence of such a certificate characterizes strong infeasibility, not weak infeasibility, for this semidefinite equality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PSD adjoint image with a negative pairing against the right-hand side is directly checkable evidence that the semidefinite equality system is strongly infeasible.
assumptions_latex: The spaces use their standard Euclidean and trace inner products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A^*y\succeq0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\) certify infeasibility.

children.title: Strict Separation Certificates
children.top_down_role: Hyperplane witnesses based on positive separation from the feasible affine space.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Separation Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric separation certificates for affine matrix spaces and the PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A_0,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb S^n\) and \(L=A_0+\operatorname{span}\{A_1,\ldots,A_m\}\). A strict separation certificate for \(L\) and \(\mathbb S_+^n\) is a matrix \(Y\in\mathbb S^n\) satisfying
\[Y\succeq0,\qquad \langle Y,A_i\rangle=0\quad(i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \langle Y,A_0\rangle<0.\]
For such a certificate,
\[\langle Y,W\rangle<0\leq\langle Y,X\rangle\qquad\text{for all }W\in L\text{ and }X\in\mathbb S_+^n.\]
Its existence certifies strong infeasibility of the affine semidefinite system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PSD matrix annihilating every affine direction and pairing negatively with the offset strictly separates the affine space from the PSD cone and certifies strong infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The pairing is the trace inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle Y,W\rangle<0\leq\langle Y,X\rangle\) for all \(W\in L\) and \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b\notin\operatorname{cl}\mathcal A(\mathbb S_+^n)\iff\exists y:\mathcal A^*y\succeq0,\ \langle b,y\rangle<0\).

notation.meaning: Adjoint of the constraint map under trace and Euclidean inner products.
Cone of positive semidefinite symmetric matrices.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strong-infeasibility regime for an equality-form SDP feasibility system.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Infeasibility Certificates p. 106
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\mathcal A(\mathbb S_+^n)\). The system \(\mathcal A(X)=b\), \(X\succeq0\), is strongly infeasible exactly when \(b\notin\operatorname{cl}K\). In that regime, strict separation of \(b\) from \(K\) is equivalent to an ordinary conic Farkas certificate: there exists \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \(\mathcal A^*y\succeq0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\). Conversely, any such \(y\) strictly separates \(b\) from every \(\mathcal A(X)\) with \(X\succeq0\), and therefore certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong SDP infeasibility, strict separation from the closed image cone, and existence of an ordinary Farkas multiplier are equivalent.

children.top_down_role: Sequences exposing successively smaller containing faces.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_i=F_{i-1}\cap Z_i^\perp\), followed by \(\mathcal A^*y_{k+1}\in F_k^*\) and \(\langle b,y_{k+1}\rangle<0\), certifies \(H\cap\mathbb S_+^n=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Successively exposed faces containing every possible feasible matrix.
Exposing matrix at reduction step i.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A facial-reduction infeasibility certificate consists of multipliers \(y_1,\ldots,y_{k+1}\) and faces \(F_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq F_k\). For \(1\le i\le k\), require \(Z_i=\mathcal A^*y_i\in F_{i-1}^*\), \(\langle b,y_i\rangle=0\), and \(F_i=F_{i-1}\cap Z_i^\perp\). These relations imply that every matrix in \(H\cap F_{i-1}\) lies in \(F_i\). If additionally \(\mathcal A^*y_{k+1}\in F_k^*\) and \(\langle b,y_{k+1}\rangle<0\), then \(H\cap F_k=\varnothing\), hence \(H\cap\mathbb S_+^n=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exposing multipliers successively restrict all feasible candidates to smaller faces; a final strict separator over the last face certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Facial-Reduction Certificate Sequences

children.title: Exact Extended-Dual Certificate Family
children.top_down_role: Lifted dual systems restoring exact status and attainment.

children.title: Extended-Dual Certificates
children.top_down_role: Lifted dual representations designed to recover exact conic status.

assumptions_latex: The original equality-form SDP data are finite-dimensional.
Auxiliary variables are constrained by linear equations and positive-semidefinite blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility of the lifted certificate system is equivalent to the certified primal-dual assertion after projection onto the original data.

notation.meaning: Tuple of original and auxiliary certificate variables.
Linear map defining the lifted equalities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract specification of an exact lifted SDP certificate family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended-dual certificate is a finite tuple \(u=(y,W_1,",W_r)\) satisfying a lifted semidefinite system \(\mathcal E(u)=e\) and \(W_i\succeq0\) for \(1\le i\le r\), where eliminating the auxiliary matrices \(W_i\) yields the desired dual bound or infeasibility assertion for the original SDP. Exactness requires both directions: every feasible lifted tuple gives a valid original assertion, and whenever that assertion is true, at least one lifted tuple exists. Thus certificate verification uses only linear equalities, trace inner products, and positive-semidefiniteness tests, without a constraint qualification for the original formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended dual replaces a potentially nonattained ordinary certificate by a finite lifted semidefinite witness whose projection is exact.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Dual Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source or concrete extended-dual construction supports the asserted exact projection equivalence. The tuple contains malformed text in place of an ellipsis, and the unspecified map and auxiliary constraints do not define a checkable certificate family.

children.title: Ramana-Type Certificates
children.top_down_role: Canonical extended systems specialized to semidefinite programming.

assumptions_latex: The primal SDP is given in finite-dimensional equality form.
The Ramana lift is formed for that primal data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Ramana-type lifted dual has the primal value and attains it whenever that value is finite; its strict negative-bound specialization yields an exact infeasibility witness.

notation.meaning: Optimal value of the primal SDP.
Feasible set of the Ramana-type extended dual.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional Ramana extended dual; its explicit block recursion requires source selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-dimensional SDP, the Ramana-type extended dual augments the ordinary dual multiplier with a finite sequence of positive-semidefinite blocks encoding the facial-reduction tangent relations. For every lifted feasible point, its objective is a valid dual bound. Conversely, if the primal optimal value \(p^*\) is finite, then there exists \(u\in D_R\) whose objective equals \(p^*\); hence the lifted dual attains the primal value even when the ordinary dual does not. Applied to a homogeneous normalization of feasibility, an attained strictly negative lifted objective is an exact, finitely checkable infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ramana’s lift encodes facial reduction inside an SDP and supplies an attained exact dual value or infeasibility witness without Slater regularity.
knowledge_statements.title: Ramana-Type Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-attainment theorem and its infeasibility specialization depend on the precise Ramana-type recursion, normalization, and hypotheses. Those constraints and an authoritative theorem locator are absent.

children.title: Exact-Attainment Restoration
children.top_down_role: Attainment behavior recovered through lifted certificate spaces.

assumptions_latex: The primal SDP is feasible and has finite optimal value \(p^*\).
An exact extended dual is constructed from the same data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{u\in D_E}\varphi(u)=p^*\) and the maximum is attained.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the exact extended dual.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment property of an exact facial-reduction-based extended dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p^*\in\mathbb R\) be the optimal value of a feasible primal SDP, and let \(D_E\) be the feasible set of an exact extended dual obtained by encoding a complete facial-reduction chain. Weak duality gives \(\varphi(u)\le p^*\) for every \(u\in D_E\). Exact-attainment restoration means that there is a lifted feasible point \(u^*\in D_E\) satisfying \(\varphi(u^*)=p^*\). Consequently, the extended dual has zero duality gap and an optimizer even when the ordinary dual has the same supremum but no maximizer, or requires a constraint qualification to guarantee attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete facial-reduction lift restores an attained dual optimizer equal in value to the finite feasible primal optimum.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Attainment Restoration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Exact attainment is construction-dependent. Without a defined extended dual and a theorem-level source, the stated equality and attainment conclusion cannot be reliably reviewed.

children.title: Lift-Size Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Representation costs associated with additional certificate variables and cone blocks.

assumptions_latex: Each nontrivial facial-reduction step strictly lowers the rank of the supporting face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The facial-reduction depth satisfies \(d\le n\), so standard sequential lifts use \(O(n)\) auxiliary PSD blocks, while shorter instance-specific lifts may use \(O(d)\).

notation.meaning: Length of a shortest facial-reduction sequence.
Matrix order of the original PSD cone.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block-count comparison for sequential facial-reduction lifts; encoding size is formulation-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) is represented by positive-semidefinite matrices supported on a subspace. A nonredundant facial-reduction step strictly decreases that subspace dimension, so a reduction sequence has length \(d\le n\). An extended dual that introduces a constant number of auxiliary semidefinite blocks per reduction step therefore uses \(O(d)\) such blocks and at most \(O(n)\) blocks in the worst case. Universal lifts avoid knowing \(d\) beforehand but may realize this worst-case size; instance-adapted lifts can be smaller when the singularity degree is low.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential exact lifts need blocks proportional to facial-reduction depth, at most linear in matrix order, while instance-specific lifts can be smaller.
knowledge_statements.title: Lift-Size Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The facial-reduction depth bound is plausible, but the auxiliary-block count depends on the selected extended-dual construction and what counts as a block. A construction-specific source is required for this complexity claim.

children.title: Reformulation-Normal-Form Certificate Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Row-operation and congruence-based structural certificates.

children.title: Elementary-Reformulation Certificates
children.top_down_role: Structural witnesses obtained through admissible row operations or congruence transformations.

assumptions_latex: The system is \(A_i\mathbin{\bullet}X=b_i\) for \(1\le i\le m\), with \(X\succeq0\).
Congruence matrices used in reformulation are nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite sequence of invertible equation transformations and congruences ending in an explicit PSD contradiction certifies infeasibility of the original system.

notation.meaning: Trace inner product of symmetric matrices.
Invertible transformation of the equality system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-preserving row operations and congruences terminating in a visible PSD contradiction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An elementary-reformulation certificate records finitely many operations of two types: replace the equality vector by \(G(\mathcal A(X)-b)=0\) with invertible \(G\), and replace \(X\) by \(TYT^{\mathsf T}\) with nonsingular \(T\). Both operations preserve feasibility and can be checked directly. The terminal reformulation must contain an explicit contradiction valid for every \(Y\succeq0\), for example a constraint \(Z\mathbin{\bullet}Y=-1\) with \(Z\succeq0\). The operation list together with the terminal matrix \(Z\) is therefore a finite certificate that the original semidefinite system is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible row operations and congruences preserve feasibility; reaching a visibly impossible PSD equation gives a checkable infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Elementary-Reformulation Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasibility-preserving operations and terminal PSD contradiction are mathematically plausible and fit a certificate leaf, but no cited normal-form or elementary-reformulation result establishes that this is the intended certificate class.

children.title: Normal-Form Certificates
children.top_down_role: Canonical block patterns exposing feasibility pathologies.

assumptions_latex: The SDP feasibility system has been transformed by feasibility-preserving elementary reformulations.
The terminal constraints are displayed in a specified semidefinite normal form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The terminal normal-form obstruction, together with the reversible transformation data, certifies the same infeasibility classification for the original system.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract certificate schema pending selection of a precise SDP infeasibility normal form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A normal-form certificate consists of reversible reformulation data and a terminal system \(\widehat{\mathcal A}(Y)=\widehat b\), \(Y\succeq0\), whose block structure satisfies the chosen normal-form obstruction. Verification has two parts: each recorded transformation must preserve feasibility in both directions, and the displayed terminal blocks must satisfy every equality and rank condition required by that obstruction. If the terminal form is a strong-infeasibility form, it yields a strict separator; if it is a weak-infeasibility form, it must instead exhibit infeasibility together with zero distance from the affine space to the PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normal-form certificate combines reversible transformations with a canonical terminal obstruction distinguishing strong from weak SDP infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Form Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record does not select or state a particular SDP normal form, its block and rank conditions, or its strong- and weak-infeasibility criteria. Consequently it is not yet a checkable normal-form certificate.

children.title: Reformulation-to-Normal-Form Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections between transformation sequences and their resulting canonical structures.

assumptions_latex: Only invertible equation transformations and nonsingular matrix congruences are used.
A fixed terminal normal-form convention has been selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Elementary reformulation certificates and terminal normal-form certificates translate into one another while preserving feasibility and the strong-versus-weak infeasibility regime.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bidirectional certificate translation for a fixed, explicitly chosen normal-form convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be a finite composition of invertible equation transformations and nonsingular congruences, and suppose \(R(\mathcal F)=\widehat{\mathcal F}\). Then \(X\) is feasible for \(\mathcal F\) if and only if the corresponding transformed matrix is feasible for \(\widehat{\mathcal F}\). Hence the list defining \(R\), followed by the terminal normal-form obstruction, is an elementary-reformulation certificate. Conversely, a normal-form certificate becomes an elementary certificate by expanding \(R\) into its individual operations. Because these maps are homeomorphisms on the relevant finite-dimensional spaces, the correspondence preserves both infeasibility and the distinction between positive and zero separation distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expanding or composing reversible reformulations translates between operational certificates and normal-form certificates without changing the infeasibility regime.
knowledge_statements.title: Reformulation-to-Normal-Form Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The correspondence cannot be evaluated until a precise terminal normal form and its allowed transformations are fixed. The preservation of zero versus positive separation also requires a formulation-specific theorem or argument supported by a source.

children.title: Weak-Infeasibility Certificates
children.top_down_role: Finite structural witnesses for nonseparated infeasible systems.

assumptions_latex: \(K=\mathcal A(\mathbb S_+^n)\) for a linear map \(\mathcal A:\mathbb S^n\to\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak infeasibility is equivalent to \(b\in\operatorname{cl}K\setminus K\), or equivalently to infeasibility with no multiplier \(y\) satisfying \(\mathcal A^*y\succeq0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\).

notation.meaning: Linear image of the PSD cone.
Distance induced by any norm on the finite-dimensional ambient space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Image-cone characterization of weak infeasibility for equality-form SDP.

source_refs.locator: 3.4 Infeasibility Certificates p. 106
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system is weakly infeasible precisely when \(b\notin K\) but \(b\in\operatorname{cl}K\). Equivalently, it has no feasible matrix, while \(\operatorname{dist}(b,K)=0\); thus there are matrices \(X_j\succeq0\) with \(\mathcal A(X_j)\to b\). In this regime no ordinary strict Farkas certificate exists: there is no \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) satisfying \(\mathcal A^*y\succeq0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle<0\). A finite structural certificate must therefore encode additional facial-reduction or normal-form information rather than strict separation alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak infeasibility means the right-hand side lies in the closure, but not the image, of the PSD cone; strict Farkas separation is impossible.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Infeasibility Certificates

source_witnesses.locator: 3.4 Infeasibility Certificates p. 106
source_witnesses.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives the standard image-closure condition for weak infeasibility, not the finite structural witness required by the immutable Weak-Infeasibility Certificates container. Its final sentence merely says that additional certificate information is necessary.

children.top_down_role: Failure modes of ordinary primal-dual SDP formulations and their geometric mechanisms.

children.title: Positive Duality-Gap Regimes
children.top_down_role: Feasible primal-dual pairs with separated limiting values.

assumptions_latex: The dual is \(\sup\{b^{\mathsf T}y:C-\mathcal A^*y\succeq0\}\), and both sides are feasible with finite values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regime has a positive duality gap exactly when \(0<p^*-d^*<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical primal-minimization and dual-maximization SDP pair without a regularity assumption.

source_refs.locator: 2 Semidefinite Optimization p. 3

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Duality Theory p. 7

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(p^*=\inf\{C\mathbin{\bullet}X:\mathcal A(X)=b,\ X\succeq0\}\) and \(d^*=\sup\{b^{\mathsf T}y:C-\mathcal A^*y\succeq0\}\). Weak duality always gives \(d^*\le p^*\). A positive duality-gap regime occurs when both feasible sets are nonempty, both values are finite, and \(p^*-d^*>0\). This definition concerns limiting optimal values and does not require either value to be attained. Slater-type regularity on either appropriate side excludes this regime by forcing equality of the two values under the standard finite-value hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-gap SDP has feasible primal and dual problems with finite limiting values, but the primal infimum strictly exceeds the dual supremum.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Duality-Gap Regimes

children.title: Finite but Unattained Optima
children.top_down_role: Finite limiting values without feasible optimizers on one side.

assumptions_latex: The canonical primal-dual SDP pair has at least one finite optimal value.
The feasible set on the side under consideration is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite nonattainment means a finite infimum or supremum exists but the corresponding argmin or argmax set is empty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment on either side of a finite-dimensional canonical SDP pair.

source_refs.locator: 2 Semidefinite Optimization p. 3

source_refs.locator: 1.5.1 Duality theory p. 24

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the primal feasible set \(P=\{X\succeq0:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\), finite primal nonattainment means \(p^*=\inf_{X\in P}C\mathbin{\bullet}X\in\mathbb R\) but no \(X^*\in P\) satisfies \(C\mathbin{\bullet}X^*=p^*\). Equivalently, an optimizing sequence exists while every feasible point has strictly larger objective. Finite dual nonattainment is defined analogously: \(d^*=\sup_{y\in D}b^{\mathsf T}y\in\mathbb R\), but no \(y^*\in D\) realizes \(d^*\). Either phenomenon may occur independently of whether \(p^*=d^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SDP optimum is finitely unattained when its infimum or supremum is finite and approached by feasible points but achieved by none.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite but Unattained Optima

children.title: Nonclosed Linear Images of PSD Cones
children.top_down_role: Image-closure failures underlying gaps and weak infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Linear Images of PSD Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-dimensional PSD example exhibiting image nonclosedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the linear map \(\mathcal L:\mathbb S^2\to\mathbb R^2\) by \(\mathcal L(X)=(X_{11},X_{12})\). Then
\[
\mathcal L(\mathbb S_+^2)=\{(a,b):a>0,\ b\in\mathbb R\}\cup\{(0,0)\}.
\]
Indeed, positive semidefiniteness permits arbitrary \(b\) when \(a>0\), after choosing \(X_{22}\ge b^2/a\), whereas \(a=0\) forces \(b=0\). Consequently this image is not closed: \((k^{-1},1)\) belongs to it for every positive integer \(k\), but its limit \((0,1)\) does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear projection of the two-by-two PSD cone contains every point with positive first coordinate but omits certain boundary limits, so it is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal L(\mathbb S_+^2)\) is not closed.

notation.meaning: cone of real two-by-two positive semidefinite matrices

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically correct and fits the failure container, but it has no citation and includes proof-style justification that should be removed after sourcing.

children.title: SDP Normal-Form Regularity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Canonical structural patterns separating regular and pathological systems.

children.title: Good SDP Normal Forms
children.top_down_role: Canonical structures associated with regular dual behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Good SDP Normal Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pataki-type regularity conditions relative to a maximum-rank slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\sum_{i=1}^m x_iA_i\preceq B\), transformed so that a maximum-rank slack is \(Z=\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0)\). Partition every \(V\in L:=\operatorname{span}\{A_1,\ldots,A_m,B\}\) conformally as \(V=\begin{psmallmatrix}V_{11}&V_{12}\\V_{12}^{T}&V_{22}\end{psmallmatrix}\). The system is in good normal form when: (i) every \(V\in L\) satisfying \(V_{22}=0\) also satisfies \(V_{12}=0\); and (ii) some \(U\in L^\perp\) has lower-right block \(U_{22}\succ0\). These conditions exclude the block obstruction responsible for pathological dual behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a maximum-rank slack, a good normal form eliminates unsupported off-diagonal blocks and admits a positive-definite complementary lower block.
assumptions_latex: \(Z=\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0)\) is a maximum-rank slack after an invertible reformulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed block predicates constitute the good normal-form conditions.

notation.meaning: linear span of the constraint matrices and right-hand side

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the leaf, but the precise two-part normal-form characterization and reformulation hypotheses require an inspectable authoritative source.

children.title: Bad SDP Normal Forms
children.top_down_role: Canonical structures exposing gaps, nonattainment, or unstable status.

knowledge_statements.title: Bad SDP Normal Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Block obstruction relative to a maximum-rank slack.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\sum_{i=1}^m x_iA_i\preceq B\), let a maximum-rank slack be \(Z=\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0)\), and partition each \(V\in L:=\operatorname{span}\{A_1,\ldots,A_m,B\}\) conformally. A bad normal-form witness is a matrix
\[
V=\begin{pmatrix}V_{11}&V_{12}\\V_{12}^{T}&V_{22}\end{pmatrix}\in L
\]
with \(V_{22}\succeq0\) and \(\operatorname{range}(V_{12}^{T})\nsubseteq\operatorname{range}(V_{22})\). Existence of such a witness is the block obstruction characterizing a badly behaved semidefinite system under the corresponding normal-form theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bad normal form contains a span matrix whose positive-semidefinite lower block cannot support its off-diagonal block.
assumptions_latex: \(Z=\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0)\) is a maximum-rank slack after an invertible reformulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence of \(V\) with the displayed range obstruction is a bad normal-form certificate.

notation.meaning: span of the system matrices and right-hand side
blocks induced by the range and nullspace of the maximum-rank slack

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The range obstruction is plausible and appropriately typed as a condition, but its claimed characterization of bad behavior requires the exact normal-form theorem and hypotheses.

children.title: Normal-Form Pathology Boundary
children.top_down_role: Structural features distinguishing regular forms from pathological forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Form Pathology Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic boundary between well-behaved and pathological SDP systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a feasible semidefinite system in maximum-rank-slack form with \(Z=\operatorname{diag}(I_r,0)\). The regular side of the boundary satisfies both good conditions: zero lower-right block forces zero off-diagonal block throughout \(L\), and \(L^\perp\) contains a matrix positive definite on \(\ker Z\). The pathological side is entered exactly when a bad witness \(V\in L\) exists with \(V_{22}\succeq0\) but \(\operatorname{range}(V_{12}^{T})\nsubseteq\operatorname{range}(V_{22})\). Under the normal-form characterization, these alternatives separate well-behaved from badly behaved systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The boundary is crossed when an off-diagonal block extends beyond the range supported by its positive-semidefinite lower block.
assumptions_latex: The system is feasible and has been put into maximum-rank-slack normal form.
Behavior is interpreted under the finite-dimensional SDP normal-form characterization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The good block conditions and the bad range obstruction describe opposite sides of the normal-form regularity boundary.

notation.meaning: span defining the normal-form block test

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf, but the asserted exact separation of well- and badly behaved systems depends on an uncited theorem and an explicit definition of those behaviors.

children.title: Facial Reduction for SDP
children.top_down_role: Certificate, representation, and regularization families associated with minimal-face discovery.

children.title: Facial-Reduction Certificate
children.top_down_role: Exposing objects and alternative systems supporting face restriction.

children.title: Exposing-Matrix Certificates
children.top_down_role: PSD exposing objects identifying proper containing faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposing-Matrix Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single PSD matrix exposing a proper face containing the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\) be nonempty. A nonzero matrix \(Z=\mathcal A^*y\succeq0\) with \(b^Ty=0\) certifies that every feasible matrix lies in the proper exposed face
\[
F=\mathbb S_+^n\cap Z^\perp=\{X\succeq0:\langle Z,X\rangle=0\}.
\]
Consequently, replacing the ambient cone by \(F\) preserves the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero PSD adjoint image orthogonal to the right-hand side exposes a proper PSD face containing every feasible matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\subseteq F\subsetneq\mathbb S_+^n\).

notation.meaning: trace-inner-product adjoint of the constraint map

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

children.title: Alternative-System Certificates
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary conic systems distinguishing strict feasibility from reducibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Alternative-System Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite alternative for strict feasibility versus facial reducibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\{X\succeq0:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\ne\varnothing\). Exactly one of the following holds: (i) there exists \(X\succ0\) satisfying \(\mathcal A(X)=b\); or (ii) there exists \(y\in\mathbb R^m\) such that \(Z:=\mathcal A^*y\succeq0\), \(Z\ne0\), and \(b^Ty=0\). In case (ii), the pair \((y,Z)\) is directly checkable and certifies both failure of strict feasibility and containment of the feasible set in \(\mathbb S_+^n\cap Z^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible SDP system, either a positive-definite feasible matrix exists or a nonzero PSD adjoint certificate exposes a reducing face.
assumptions_latex: The affine PSD feasibility system is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict feasibility and the displayed nonzero alternative certificate are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

children.title: Multi-Stage Exposure Certificates
children.top_down_role: Nested exposure families for non-singly-exposed minimal faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-Stage Exposure Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A facial-reduction sequence certifying nested containment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F_0=\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(\mathcal F=\{X\in F_0:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\) be nonempty. A length-\(d\) exposure certificate consists of nonzero matrices \(Z_i\in F_{i-1}^*\) satisfying \(\langle Z_i,X\rangle=0\) for every \(X\in\mathcal F\), with
\[
F_i=F_{i-1}\cap Z_i^\perp,
\qquad i=1,\ldots,d.
\]
These conditions certify \(\mathcal F\subseteq F_i\subsetneq F_{i-1}\) at every stage. If \(F_d\) is separately established to be the minimal face containing \(\mathcal F\), the sequence is a multi-stage certificate of that minimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence of relative-dual exposing matrices certifies nested proper faces containing the feasible set and, when minimality is established, certifies its minimal face.
assumptions_latex: Every exposure is taken relative to the current face.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\subseteq F_d\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_0\), with \(F_d\) minimal when separately established.

notation.meaning: dual cone of the current face in its linear span

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

children.title: Minimal-Face Representations
children.top_down_role: Nullspace, range-space, and reduced-coordinate representations of PSD faces.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Face Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Range-space and reduced-coordinate descriptions of PSD minimal faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F\) be a face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\). There exist a subspace \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and a full-column-rank matrix \(V\) with \(\operatorname{range}(V)=U\) such that
\[
F=\{X\succeq0:\operatorname{range}(X)\subseteq U\}
 =\{VYV^T:Y\in\mathbb S_+^r\},
\]
where \(r=\dim U\). Equivalently, if the columns of \(W\) span \(U^\perp\), then \(F=\{X\succeq0:XW=0\}\). For a nonempty feasible set, its minimal containing face has this representation with \(U\) equal to the span of feasible ranges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every PSD face is determined by a range subspace and is isomorphic to a smaller PSD cone through a full-column-rank coordinate matrix.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is nonempty when its minimal face is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The range, nullspace, and reduced-coordinate descriptions define the same PSD face.

notation.meaning: basis matrix for the orthogonal complement of U

children.title: Slater Restoration by Face Restriction
children.top_down_role: Regularity recovery after replacing the ambient cone by the minimal face.

knowledge_statements.title: Slater Restoration by Face Restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative-interior regularity on the minimal feasible face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\) be nonempty, and let \(F_{\min}\) be the minimal face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) containing \(\mathcal F\). Then
\[
\mathcal F\cap\operatorname{ri}(F_{\min})\ne\varnothing.
\]
Hence replacing \(X\in\mathbb S_+^n\) by \(X\in F_{\min}\) restores Slater feasibility relative to \(\operatorname{span}(F_{\min})\). If \(F_{\min}=\{VYV^T:Y\succeq0\}\) with \(V\) full column rank, some feasible reduced matrix satisfies \(Y\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting a nonempty SDP feasibility system to its minimal PSD face yields a feasible point in that face’s relative interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\cap\operatorname{ri}(F_{\min})\ne\varnothing\), equivalently the reduced system has a positive-definite feasible coordinate matrix.

notation.meaning: minimal PSD face containing the feasible set

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Facial structure, nondegeneracy and strict complementarity p. 37

children.title: Facial-Reduction Variant Family
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral-sensitive, sparse, symmetric, and numerically approximate variants.

children.title: Partial Facial Reduction
children.top_down_role: Face reduction stopped before complete minimal-face identification.

knowledge_statements.title: Partial Facial Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Early-terminated facial reduction producing a valid intermediate face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(F_0=\mathbb S_+^n\), a feasible affine system, and a stage limit \(q\), repeat for \(i=1,\ldots,q\): find a nonzero valid exposing matrix \(Z_i\in F_{i-1}^*\) orthogonal to every feasible point, and set \(F_i=F_{i-1}\cap Z_i^\perp\). Stop earlier if the restricted system has a point in \(\operatorname{ri}(F_i)\), or if no exposing certificate is found. Output the final face \(F_j\). It preserves the feasible set, although early termination need not identify the minimal face or restore Slater feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partial facial reduction performs only a limited number of valid exposure steps, preserving feasibility but possibly stopping before the minimal face.
assumptions_latex: The starting affine PSD system is feasible.
Each accepted exposing matrix is exactly valid for the current feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output satisfies \(\mathcal F\subseteq F_j\subseteq\mathbb S_+^n\), but may satisfy \(F_j\supsetneq F_{\min}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm is internally coherent and preserves the feasible set when its certificates are valid, but “partial facial reduction” and its stopping convention require a specific source.

children.title: Approximate Facial Reduction
children.top_down_role: Numerically tolerant face identification for perturbed or noisy systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Facial Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based numerical approximation of facial exposure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given tolerances \(\varepsilon,\delta>0\) and a current face \(F\), seek \(Z\in F^*\) normalized by \(\|Z\|_F=1\) such that the affine-system residual defining an exposing certificate is at most \(\varepsilon\) and \(|\langle Z,X\rangle|\le\varepsilon\) for the represented feasible constraints. Compute an eigenspace \(U\) associated with eigenvalues of \(Z\) not exceeding \(\delta\), and replace \(F\) by the PSD face supported on \(U\). Iterate until no accepted certificate is found. The output is approximate: without error bounds or spectral separation it need not contain the exact feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate facial reduction uses residual and eigenvalue tolerances to estimate a smaller face, but exact containment requires certified errors and spectral separation.
assumptions_latex: A numerical residual model for the alternative system is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a numerically reduced face; exact facial containment is not guaranteed solely by tolerance tests.

notation.meaning: estimated nullspace support of the exposing matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Approximate facial reduction is not a canonical single algorithm here; the certificate residual, represented constraints, spectral rule, and error guarantees are insufficiently defined without a source.

children.title: Structure-Aware Facial Reduction
children.top_down_role: Reductions preserving sparsity, symmetry, block structure, or polyhedral components.

knowledge_statements.title: Structure-Aware Facial Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facial reduction constrained to a structure-preserving matrix subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal S\subseteq\mathbb S^n\) be a prescribed linear structure space containing all model matrices. Starting from a structure-compatible face \(F_0\), at stage \(i\) solve the facial-reduction alternative with the additional restriction \(Z_i\in\mathcal S\cap F_{i-1}^*\). If a nonzero valid certificate is found, set \(F_i=F_{i-1}\cap Z_i^\perp\) and represent this face using structure-compatible coordinates; otherwise stop. Every accepted exact certificate preserves the feasible set. Failure to find a structured certificate does not imply that the current face is minimal, because an unstructured exposing direction may still exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structure-aware facial reduction restricts exposing matrices and coordinates to a chosen model subspace, preserving structure but possibly missing valid reductions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal S\) is a fixed linear subspace compatible with the model.
Every accepted certificate is exactly orthogonal to the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted steps preserve feasibility and structure, but structured termination need not certify global minimality.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed structured restriction is plausible, but the relevant structure class, compatibility conditions, coordinate construction, and termination interpretation require a cited algorithmic framework.

children.title: Variant Accuracy Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural and numerical compromises among incomplete, approximate, or specialized reductions.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\).
A vector \(y\) and matrix \(Z\succeq0\) satisfy \(\|\mathcal A^*y-Z\|_F\leq\delta\) and \(|\langle b,y\rangle|\leq\eta\).
The candidate feasible matrix satisfies \(X\in\mathcal F\) and \(\|X\|_F\leq R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[|\langle Z,X\rangle|\leq \eta+\delta R.\]

notation.meaning: Linear constraint map and its adjoint.
A bound on the feasible matrix norm.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies the certificate-accuracy loss incurred by approximate rather than exact facial reduction.

source_refs.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every \(X\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \(\|X\|_F\leq R\) obeys \[|\langle Z,X\rangle|\leq\eta+\delta R.\] Thus exact certificates, for which \(\delta=\eta=0\), give exact orthogonality to \(Z\), whereas approximate certificates give an orthogonality error bounded by the certificate residuals and the norm scale \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate exposing certificate violates facial orthogonality by at most its scalar residual plus its matrix residual times the feasible-set norm scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Variant Accuracy Tradeoffs

source_witnesses.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

children.title: Singularity Degree
children.top_down_role: Depth of facial regularization and its relationships with degeneracy, error bounds, and certificates.

children.title: Low Singularity-Degree Regimes
children.top_down_role: Strictly feasible and singly exposed minimal-face regimes.

children.title: Degree-Zero Regimes
children.top_down_role: Strictly feasible systems requiring no facial-reduction exposure.

assumptions_latex: The nonempty system is \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\).
Singularity degree counts facial-reduction steps before relative strict feasibility is reached.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathcal F\cap\mathbb S_{++}^n\neq\varnothing.\]

notation.meaning: Singularity degree of the feasibility system.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convention that an already strictly feasible system has singularity degree zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system is in the degree-zero regime precisely when no proper-face reduction is required. Equivalently, its affine constraints satisfy Slater's condition in the original cone: \[\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists X\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\ \text{such that}\ \mathcal A(X)=b.\] In this case the minimal face of \(\mathbb S_+^n\) containing \(\mathcal F\) is the entire cone \(\mathbb S_+^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singularity degree zero means that the original semidefinite feasibility system already has a positive definite feasible matrix.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Zero Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition matches the degree-zero leaf and is correct under the stated convention, but no source with an inspectable locator is supplied. An authoritative singularity-degree definition is required to confirm the zero-step convention.

children.title: Degree-One Regimes
children.top_down_role: Systems whose minimal face is reached through a single exposure.

assumptions_latex: The nonempty system is \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\) and is not strictly feasible.
A facial-reduction step uses a nonzero \(y\) with \(Z=\mathcal A^*y\succeq0\) and \(\langle b,y\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists y:\ \mathcal F\cap\operatorname{ri}(\mathbb S_+^n\cap Z^\perp)\neq\varnothing,\quad Z=\mathcal A^*y\neq0.\]

notation.meaning: Exposing matrix generated by a multiplier.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes systems whose minimal feasible face is exposed in one reduction step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The system has singularity degree one if and only if it fails Slater's condition in \(\mathbb S_+^n\), but there exists a multiplier \(y\) such that \(Z=\mathcal A^*y\succeq0\), \(Z\neq0\), and \(\langle b,y\rangle=0\), for which \[\mathcal F\cap\operatorname{ri}(\mathbb S_+^n\cap Z^\perp)\neq\varnothing.\] The face \(\mathbb S_+^n\cap Z^\perp\) is then the minimal face containing \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degree one means strict feasibility fails initially, but one valid exposing certificate reaches a face where relative strict feasibility holds.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-One Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-step characterization fits the degree-one leaf, but it depends on the precise facial-reduction and singularity-degree conventions. No source is supplied to validate the multiplier conditions or the equivalence with reaching the minimal face in one step.

children.title: Zero-to-One Degree Transition
children.top_down_role: Loss of strict feasibility leading to a singly exposed minimal face.

assumptions_latex: Singularity degree zero denotes strict feasibility, and degree one denotes one necessary exposing reduction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F_t)=0\ \text{for}\ t>0,\qquad \operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F_0)=1.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-dimensional family exhibits an exact degree-zero to degree-one boundary at \(t=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(t>0\), the matrix \(\operatorname{diag}(t,1)\) belongs to \(\mathcal F_t\cap\mathbb S_{++}^2\), so \(\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F_t)=0\). At \(t=0\), positive semidefiniteness forces \(X_{12}=0\), and hence \(\mathcal F_0=\{\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\}\). The matrix \(Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) exposes its minimal face in one step, so \(\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F_0)=1\). Thus singularity degree can change discontinuously under vanishing data perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive diagonal perturbation gives strict feasibility, while its zero limit forces a proper face and raises singularity degree from zero to one.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-to-One Degree Transition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The parameterized example is mathematically coherent and failure_boundary is appropriate for the transition leaf, but it has no cited source. A specific perturbation or singularity-degree example locator is required.

children.title: Higher Singularity-Degree Regimes
children.top_down_role: Nested exposure regimes requiring multiple reductions.

assumptions_latex: The nonempty spectrahedron is \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\).
A facial-reduction chain is \(F_0=\mathbb S_+^n\) and \(F_i=F_{i-1}\cap Z_i^\perp\), with each \(Z_i\in F_{i-1}^*\) valid for \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F)\geq2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \text{every chain reaching a face }F_k\text{ with }\mathcal F\cap\operatorname{ri}(F_k)\neq\varnothing\text{ has }k\geq2.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines higher-degree systems through the minimum length of a nested facial-reduction chain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The singularity degree \(\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F)\) is the smallest \(k\) for which there exist valid exposing matrices \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_k\) generating nested faces \[F_0=\mathbb S_+^n,\qquad F_i=F_{i-1}\cap Z_i^\perp,\] such that \(\mathcal F\cap\operatorname{ri}(F_k)\neq\varnothing\). A higher singularity-degree regime is one with \(\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F)\geq2\); no single valid exposing matrix reaches a face supporting relative strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-degree system requires at least two nested exposing reductions before the feasible set becomes relatively strictly feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Higher Singularity-Degree Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for this regime container, but the phrase 'valid for the feasible set' does not explicitly state all certificate conditions relative to each current face. No authoritative source is provided to fix those conditions and the chain-length convention.

children.title: Singularity-Degree Error-Bound Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Residual-to-distance degradation in singular systems.

children.title: Singularity-Degree Stratification
children.top_down_role: Organization of singular systems by facial-reduction depth.

assumptions_latex: Let \(\mathfrak P\) be a class of nonempty semidefinite feasibility systems.
Each \(P\in\mathfrak P\) has a finite singularity degree \(\operatorname{sd}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak P=\bigsqcup_{d\geq0}\mathfrak P_d,\qquad \mathfrak P_d=\{P\in\mathfrak P:\operatorname{sd}(P)=d\}.\]

notation.meaning: Stratum of systems having singularity degree exactly d.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partitions a model class by the exact number of facial reductions required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each integer \(d\geq0\), define the singularity-degree stratum \[\mathfrak P_d=\{P\in\mathfrak P:\operatorname{sd}(P)=d\}.\] Because singularity degree is single-valued, the strata are pairwise disjoint; because every system in \(\mathfrak P\) has finite degree, their union is \(\mathfrak P\). Thus \(\mathfrak P=\bigsqcup_{d\geq0}\mathfrak P_d\). This stratification indexes systems by facial-reduction depth and therefore separates the regimes used in degree-dependent local error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semidefinite systems split into disjoint strata according to the exact number of facial reductions needed to restore relative strict feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Singularity-Degree Stratification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed partition is a valid representation once finite singularity degree is assumed, and it fits the stratification leaf. However, no source supports either the relevant model-class convention or the asserted connection to degree-dependent error bounds.

children.title: Residual Error Bounds
children.top_down_role: Residual-to-distance behavior for semidefinite feasibility systems.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\neq\varnothing\) with singularity degree \(d\).
Matrices are restricted to a fixed bounded set \(B\subset\mathbb S^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{dist}(X,\mathcal F)\leq C_B\bigl(\rho(X)+\rho(X)^{2^{-d}}\bigr)\qquad(X\in B).\]

notation.meaning: Combined affine and conic feasibility residual.
Bounded region on which the estimate is uniform.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the bounded-set Hölder error-bound form commonly associated with facial-reduction depth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\rho(X)=\|\mathcal A(X)-b\|+\operatorname{dist}(X,\mathbb S_+^n).\] Under the standard bounded linear-regularity hypotheses for the terminal reduced system, every bounded set \(B\subset\mathbb S^n\) admits a constant \(C_B>0\) such that \[\operatorname{dist}(X,\mathcal F)\leq C_B\bigl(\rho(X)+\rho(X)^{2^{-d}}\bigr)\qquad\text{for all }X\in B.\] For \(d=0\), this reduces to a local Lipschitz error bound; each additional facial-reduction level may halve the guaranteed Hölder exponent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On bounded regions, feasibility distance is controlled by the residual with a Hölder exponent that can fall to two raised to minus the singularity degree.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Error Bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact Hölder exponent and error-bound conclusion require an authoritative theorem. 'Standard bounded linear-regularity hypotheses' is not an explicit hypothesis, and the asserted existence of a constant is theorem-like rather than merely a generic property. No source is supplied.

children.title: Degree-Dependent Error Degradation
children.top_down_role: Deterioration of error-bound regularity across increasing singularity degree.

assumptions_latex: For singularity degree \(d\), the available residual estimate has Hölder exponent \(\alpha_d=2^{-d}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\alpha_{d+1}=\frac{\alpha_d}{2},\qquad \rho^{\alpha_{d+1}}\geq\rho^{\alpha_d}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses degradation within the exponent hierarchy \(2^{-d}\), not a universal sharpness claim.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the facial-reduction error-bound hierarchy \(\alpha_d=2^{-d}\), increasing singularity degree from \(d\) to \(d+1\) gives \[\alpha_{d+1}=2^{-(d+1)}=\frac{\alpha_d}{2}.\] Since \(0<\rho<1\), a smaller exponent yields a larger error term: \[\rho^{\alpha_{d+1}}\geq\rho^{\alpha_d}.\] Consequently, the guaranteed residual-to-distance control weakens monotonically with facial-reduction depth, although particular structured instances may admit stronger exponents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each added reduction level halves the standard guaranteed Hölder exponent, so the same small residual permits a larger distance bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Dependent Error Degradation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic comparison is correct conditional on the assumed hierarchy, and property fits the degradation leaf. However, the optimization-specific claim that the available exponent is exactly \(2^{-d}\) is placed in the assumptions and has no supporting source.

children.title: Singularity Degree in Structured Models
children.top_down_role: Graph and data structure governing singularity in completion and realization models.

assumptions_latex: Consider full-matrix completion systems on the fixed graph \(K_2\).
For prescribed data \(M\in\mathbb S_+^2\), the feasible set is the singleton \(\mathcal F_M=\{M\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F_{I_2})=0,\qquad \operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F_{\operatorname{diag}(0,1)})=1.\]

notation.meaning: Completion feasibility set for prescribed matrix data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that graph structure alone does not determine singularity degree; numerical data also govern the minimal face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the same completion graph \(K_2\), prescribing \(M=I_2\) gives a positive definite feasible matrix and therefore \(\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F_{I_2})=0\). Prescribing \(M=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\) instead forces the feasible matrix into the proper face exposed by \(Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\), and one reduction restores relative strict feasibility, so \(\operatorname{sd}(\mathcal F_M)=1\). Hence a structured model's graph may constrain possible reduction patterns, but the graph without its data does not determine singularity degree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two completion instances with the same graph can have different singularity degrees, so both combinatorial structure and prescribed data matter.
knowledge_statements.title: Singularity Degree in Structured Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The example supports the stated boundary phenomenon and is locally relevant to structured models, but no structured-completion or singularity-degree source is cited. The convention for treating a fully prescribed matrix as a completion instance also needs source support.

children.title: Extreme-Point Rank Bounds
children.top_down_role: Rank restrictions derived from affine dimension and extremality.

assumptions_latex: The spectrahedron is \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\), where \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal A)=m\).
The matrix \(X\in\mathcal F\) is an extreme point and has rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\frac{r(r+1)}2\leq m.\]

notation.meaning: Rank of the extreme feasible matrix.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real-symmetric Barvinok–Pataki bound for extreme points of a spectrahedron.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.1 Finding an extreme point solution p. 60

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X\) is an extreme point of \(\mathcal F\) and \(r=\operatorname{rank}(X)\), then \[\frac{r(r+1)}2\leq m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extreme feasible matrix under m independent affine equations has rank r satisfying r times r plus one over two at most m.

children.title: Optimal-Solution Rank Bounds
children.top_down_role: Existence of low-rank optimizers on optimal faces.

assumptions_latex: The spectrahedron \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\) is nonempty and compact, with \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal A)=m\).
A linear objective \(\langle C,X\rangle\) is minimized over \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists X^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{X\in\mathcal F}\langle C,X\rangle:\quad \frac{r(r+1)}2\leq m,\qquad r=\operatorname{rank}(X^\star).\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact feasible-set version ensuring existence of an extreme optimal solution.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.1 Finding an extreme point solution p. 60

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exists an optimal solution \(X^\star\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{X\in\mathcal F}\langle C,X\rangle\) such that, for \(r=\operatorname{rank}(X^\star)\), \[\frac{r(r+1)}2\leq m.\] This is an existence statement and does not assert that every optimizer has rank satisfying the bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact feasible SDP with m independent equations has at least one optimal solution whose rank satisfies the Barvinok–Pataki bound.

children.title: Block Product-Cone Rank Bounds
children.top_down_role: Rank accounting across multiple PSD blocks.

children.title: Product-Cone Rank Bounds
children.top_down_role: Aggregate rank restrictions for optimization over products of PSD cones.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(\mathcal F=\{(X_1,\ldots,X_q):X_i\in\mathbb S_+^{n_i},\ \mathcal A(X_1,\ldots,X_q)=b\}\), with \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal A)=m\).
The point \((X_1,\ldots,X_q)\in\mathcal F\) is extreme, with \(r_i=\operatorname{rank}(X_i)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sum_{i=1}^q\frac{r_i(r_i+1)}2\leq m.\]

notation.meaning: Number of positive semidefinite cone blocks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-symmetric extreme-point rank bound for a Cartesian product of positive semidefinite cones.

source_refs.locator: 3.5.1 Finding an extreme point solution p. 60

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an extreme feasible point, \(\mathcal A\) must be injective on the direct sum of the spans of the minimal faces containing the blocks \(X_i\). The span associated with block \(i\) has dimension \(r_i(r_i+1)/2\). Since the direct-sum dimension cannot exceed \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal A)=m\), \[\sum_{i=1}^q\frac{r_i(r_i+1)}2\leq m.\] The inequality controls aggregate rank allocation and need not impose the same bound on every block separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an extreme point of a product-cone spectrahedron, the sum of the triangular numbers of all block ranks cannot exceed the independent constraint count.
knowledge_statements.title: Product-Cone Rank Bounds

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5.1 Finding an extreme point solution p. 60

children.title: Blockwise Rank Bounds
children.top_down_role: Separate rank restrictions assigned to individual semidefinite blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Blockwise Rank Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real symmetric block-product form at an extreme feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(r_i=\operatorname{rank}(X_i)\). Extremality requires the equality map to be injective on the product of the symmetric perturbation spaces supported on the ranges of the blocks. Consequently,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^p \frac{r_i(r_i+1)}{2}\le m.
\]
In particular, every block satisfies
\[
\frac{r_i(r_i+1)}{2}\le m
\quad\text{and hence}\quad
r_i\le \left\lfloor\frac{\sqrt{8m+1}-1}{2}\right\rfloor.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an extreme feasible point, the triangular dimensions associated with all PSD block ranks sum to at most the number of independent equalities; consequently, each block separately obeys the scalar Pataki rank bound.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(\mathcal F=\{X:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\cap\prod_{i=1}^p\mathbb S_+^{n_i}\), where \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal A)=m\).
The block tuple \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\) is an extreme point of \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(i\), \(r_i(r_i+1)/2\le m\), and hence \(r_i\le\lfloor(\sqrt{8m+1}-1)/2\rfloor\).

notation.meaning: Linear equality map acting jointly on all blocks

children.title: Cross-Block Rank Allocation
children.top_down_role: Distribution of allowable rank across coupled PSD blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Block Rank Allocation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint rank budget for extreme points of a product of PSD cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(r_i=\operatorname{rank}(X_i)\), define \(d(r)=r(r+1)/2\). The cross-block allocation condition is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^p d(r_i)=\sum_{i=1}^p\frac{r_i(r_i+1)}{2}\le m.
\]
Thus the ranks cannot be selected independently: increasing block \(i\) from rank \(r_i\) to rank \(r_i+1\) consumes \(r_i+1\) additional dimensions of the common equality budget. A rank vector violating this inequality cannot occur at an extreme point of the stated affine slice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Block ranks share one triangular-dimension budget; raising one block's rank reduces the rank capacity available to the others.
assumptions_latex: The feasible set is an affine slice of \(\prod_{i=1}^p\mathbb S_+^{n_i}\) defined by a linear equality map of rank \(m\).
The block tuple \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)\) is an extreme feasible point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rank vector satisfies \(\sum_{i=1}^p r_i(r_i+1)/2\le m\).

notation.meaning: Dimension consumed by a rank-r symmetric face

source_refs.locator: 3 The Geometry of Semidefinite Programming p. 29

source_witnesses.locator: 3 The Geometry of Semidefinite Programming p. 29

children.title: Minimal-Face-Strengthened Rank Bounds
children.top_down_role: Refinements incorporating reduced facial dimension and singularity.

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(\mathcal F=(L+b)\capb S_+^n\), and its minimal cone face is \(F_{\min}\).
The equality map is \(\mathcal A:\operatorname{span}F_{\min}\tob R^m\).
The matrix \(X\in\mathcal F\) is extreme and has rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Writing \(q=\operatorname{rank}(\mathcal A|_{[0moperatorname{span}F_{\min}})\), one has \(r(r+1)/2\le q\le m\).

notation.meaning: Minimal face of the PSD cone containing the feasible set
Effective equality rank after restriction to the minimal face
Rank of the extreme feasible matrix

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facially reduced finite-dimensional form of the extreme-point rank bound.

source_refs.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Restrict the affine equations to \(\operatorname{span}F_{\min}\) and remove dependent restrictions. If the resulting map has rank \(q\), then every extreme feasible matrix \(X\) of rank \(r\) satisfies
\[
\frac{r(r+1)}2\le q.
\]
Since \(q\le m\), this is at least as strong as the ambient Barvinok[0m–Pataki inequality. The refinement reflects equations that remain effective after facial reduction; equations constant or dependent on \(F_{\min}\) do not contribute to the rank budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After restricting equations to the minimal feasible face, the Pataki bound uses their effective rank rather than the ambient equation count.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal-Face-Strengthened Rank Bounds

children.title: Extreme-Point Geometry
children.top_down_role: Rank, tangent-space, and affine-independence viewpoints.

knowledge_statements.title: Extreme-Point Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-space characterization for an affine slice of the real PSD cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A feasible matrix \(X=UU^{\mathsf T}\) is an extreme point of \(\mathcal F\) if and only if
\[
H\in\mathbb S^r,\qquad \mathcal A(UHU^{\mathsf T})=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad H=0.
\]
Equivalently, the equality map is injective on the symmetric perturbations supported on \(\operatorname{range}(X)\). In coefficient form, the restrictions of the equality matrices to \(\operatorname{range}(X)\) span \(\mathbb S^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible PSD matrix is extreme precisely when no nonzero symmetric perturbation supported on its range preserves every affine equality.
assumptions_latex: The spectrahedron is \(\mathcal F=\{X\in\mathbb S_+^n:\mathcal A(X)=b\}\).
The feasible matrix has a factorization \(X=UU^{\mathsf T}\), where \(U\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matrix \(X\) is extreme in \(\mathcal F\) exactly when \(\ker(H\mapsto\mathcal A(UHU^{\mathsf T}))=\{0\}\) on \(\mathbb S^r\).

notation.meaning: Linear equality map defining the spectrahedron

children.title: Spectrahedral Exposure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Objective exposure and projection-induced nonexposure phenomena.

children.title: Exposed Spectrahedral Faces
children.top_down_role: Faces selected by supporting objectives in the ambient representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Exposed Spectrahedral Faces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Faces of spectrahedra before projection, in finite-dimensional real coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Every face \(F\) of a spectrahedron \(S\) is exposed. Thus there exist \(c\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) such that
\[
c^{\mathsf T}x\ge\alpha\quad\text{for every }x\in S,
\qquad
F=\{x\in S:c^{\mathsf T}x=\alpha\}.
\]
Equivalently, every face of a spectrahedron is the complete optimal set of a linear objective. This conclusion concerns affine sections of the PSD cone and need not survive linear projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every face of a spectrahedron is exposed by a supporting linear objective, although this property can fail after projection.
assumptions_latex: The set \(S=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:A_0+\sum_{j=1}^d x_jA_j\succeq0\}\) is nonempty, where \(A_0,\ldots,A_d\in\mathbb S^n\).
The subset \(F\) is a face of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(c\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) such that \(F=\{x\in S:c^{\mathsf T}x=\alpha\}\) and \(c^{\mathsf T}x\ge\alpha\) for every \(x\in S\).

notation.meaning: Spectrahedron defined by a linear matrix inequality

children.title: Nonexposed Spectrahedral Faces
children.top_down_role: Faces lacking direct realization through an ambient supporting objective.

assumptions_latex: The set under consideration is an affine section of \(\mathbb S_+^n\), not a proper linear image of one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A spectrahedron has no nonexposed faces; any claimed nonexposed face signals projection, nonclosedness, or a broader semidefinite-representable class.

notation.meaning: Affine section of the PSD cone

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The title is interpreted as the boundary separating spectrahedra from spectrahedral shadows.

source_refs.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is no face \(F\) of a spectrahedron \(S\) that is nonexposed: every such \(F\) equals the minimizer set of a linear functional on \(S\). Therefore nonexposed faces arise only after leaving the class of affine PSD sections, for example by taking a linear image. The distinction is essential: a spectrahedral shadow may be closed and convex yet possess a proper face that no supporting hyperplane exposes exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonexposed faces cannot occur in a spectrahedron itself; they become possible in projected spectrahedra, called spectrahedral shadows.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonexposed Spectrahedral Faces

source_witnesses.locator: 3.7.1 A: The faces of the semidefinite cone p. 63

children.title: Projection-Induced Nonexposure
children.top_down_role: Loss of face exposure under projection or representation changes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The spectrahedral shadow \(C\) has nonexposed singleton faces at \(q_\pm=(1/2,\pm\sqrt3/2)\).

notation.meaning: Closed unit disk, which is spectrahedral
Convex hull obtained after lifting and projection
Tangency points from p to the unit circle

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete planar illustration that linear projection need not preserve facial exposure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The disk \(D\) is spectrahedral, and \(C=\operatorname{conv}(D\cup\{p\})\) is a spectrahedral shadow through a standard convex-hull lift. The points
\[
q_\pm=\left(\frac12,\pm\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)
\]
are extreme points of \(C\). Each singleton \(\{q_\pm\}\) is a face, but its unique supporting line also contains the segment \([q_\pm,p]\). Hence no linear functional exposes \(\{q_\pm\}\), demonstrating that projection can convert exposed lifted geometry into nonexposed image faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of the unit disk and an exterior point is a spectrahedral shadow with nonexposed extreme tangency points.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Induced Nonexposure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The planar construction and nonexposure argument are plausible, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied for either the explicit counterexample or the claim that its convex hull is a spectrahedral shadow through a semidefinite lift.

children.title: Objective-Exposure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Conditions separating objective-visible faces from nonexposed faces.

assumptions_latex: The set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The subset \(F\) is a face of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The face \(F\) is objective-exposed exactly when \(F=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}c^{\mathsf T}x\) for some \(c\in\mathbb R^d\).

notation.meaning: Face being tested for objective exposure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary between faces selectable by linear objectives and nonexposed faces.

source_refs.locator: 5.3 The Optimal Value Function p. 219
source_refs.source_title: Semidefinite Optimization and Convex Algebraic Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A face \(F\) lies on the objective-exposure side of the boundary if and only if there exists \(c\in\mathbb R^d\) such that
\[
F=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}c^{\mathsf T}x.
\]
If no such \(c\) exists, then \(F\) is nonexposed and cannot be exactly the optimal set of any linear optimization problem over \(C\). Every face of a spectrahedron satisfies the condition, whereas a face of a spectrahedral shadow may fail it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A face is objective-exposed exactly when it is the complete optimizer set of some linear objective; nonexposed faces fail this test.
knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Exposure Boundary

children.title: Multiplicity of Optimal Eigenvalues
children.top_down_role: Connections between optimal ranks and eigenvalue multiplicity.

assumptions_latex: A primal-dual SDP optimum \((X,Z)\) satisfies \(X\succeq0\), \(Z\succeq0\), and \(\langle X,Z\rangle=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One has \(\operatorname{range}X\subseteq\ker Z\), so \(\operatorname{rank}X\le\operatorname{nullity}Z\); equality holds under strict complementarity.

notation.meaning: Multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue of Z

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementarity relation between primal optimal rank and dual zero-eigenvalue multiplicity.

source_refs.locator: 3.4.1 The Multiplicity of Optimal Eigenvalues p. 55

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For positive semidefinite optimal matrices, \(\langle X,Z\rangle=0\) implies \(XZ=0\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{range}X\subseteq\ker Z,
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}X\le\dim\ker Z.
\]
Thus the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue of the optimal dual slack bounds the primal optimal rank. If strict complementarity holds, meaning \(\operatorname{rank}X+\operatorname{rank}Z=n\), then
\[
\operatorname{rank}X=\dim\ker Z.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complementarity places the primal range in the dual slack's zero eigenspace; under strict complementarity their dimensions coincide.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplicity of Optimal Eigenvalues

children.title: Chordal PSD Completion
children.top_down_role: Clique-local positivity and globally completable chordal patterns.

assumptions_latex: The graph \(G=(V,E)\) is chordal and includes every loop.
A partial symmetric matrix \(a\) specifies entries on \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partial matrix has a PSD completion exactly when every maximal-clique principal matrix \(a[C]\) is PSD.

notation.meaning: Specified principal matrix on clique C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional PSD completion theorem for chordal sparsity patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A symmetric partial matrix \(a\) with chordal specification graph \(G\) admits a completion \(X\in\mathbb S_+^{|V|}\) satisfying \(X_{ij}=a_{ij}\) for every \((i,j)\in E\) if and only if
\[
a[C]\succeq0
\]
for every maximal clique \(C\) of \(G\). Because clique intersections carry the same specified entries, no additional consistency equations are required beyond agreement already encoded by the single partial matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a chordal sparsity graph, a partial symmetric matrix is PSD-completable exactly when every maximal-clique submatrix is PSD.
knowledge_statements.title: Chordal PSD Completion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The chordal PSD completion theorem is stated precisely and its theorem kind fits the leaf, but no citation or locator is supplied. An authoritative completion-theorem source is required.

children.title: Nonchordal PSD Completion
children.top_down_role: Completion behavior for sparsity graphs containing chordless cycles.

assumptions_latex: The specification graph \(G=(V,E)\) is not chordal.
The partial symmetric matrix \(a\) specifies all diagonal entries and entries indexed by \(E\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: PSD completability is equivalent to feasibility of global fill variables, while PSD conditions on the original maximal cliques alone are generally insufficient.

notation.meaning: Unspecified matrix entries serving as fill variables
Full symmetric matrix formed from specified and fill entries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global feasibility formulation for nonchordal partial PSD matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(y\) index all unspecified off-diagonal entries. The partial matrix \(a\) is PSD-completable if and only if
\[
\text{there exists }y\text{ such that }X(a,y)\succeq0.
\]
Unlike the chordal case, positivity of every fully specified principal submatrix, or of the principal matrices on the original maximal cliques, does not generally imply this feasibility condition. Constraints around chordless cycles couple the missing entries globally, so completion cannot in general be certified solely by the original clique-local PSD tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonchordal pattern, PSD completion requires globally compatible fill entries; PSD tests on the original cliques are not generally sufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonchordal PSD Completion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The global-fill representation is correct by definition, while the claimed general insufficiency of original clique tests is nontrivial and requires an inspectable source. None is supplied.

children.title: Chordal Fill Selection
children.top_down_role: Choice of added edges used to obtain a chordal extension.

assumptions_latex: The graph \(G=(V,E)\) is an arbitrary undirected specification graph.
A chordal extension is sought on the same vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A selected fill set \(F\) is valid exactly when \(G_F=(V,E\cup F)\) is chordal; completion can then be represented by PSD constraints on maximal cliques of \(G_F\).

notation.meaning: Chordal extension induced by the fill

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity condition and modeling consequence for selecting chordal fill edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A fill set \(F\subseteq\binom{V}{2}\setminus E\) is admissible when every cycle of length at least four in \(G_F=(V,E\cup F)\) has a chord. For such \(F\), introduce variables for entries on \(F\). A PSD completion of the original partial matrix exists if and only if these fill variables can be chosen so that
\[
X[C]\succeq0
\]
for every maximal clique \(C\) of \(G_F\), with shared entries identified across overlapping cliques. Different valid fills produce equivalent feasibility descriptions but different clique sizes and computational costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid fill makes the graph chordal, after which PSD completion is modeled by consistent PSD constraints on the extension's maximal cliques.
knowledge_statements.title: Chordal Fill Selection
